General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

When Your Doctor Prescribes a Visit to an Art Gallery

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars.
  • But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail.
  • In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend PaRx, Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks.

But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the Vancouver Art Gallery, and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend PaRx, Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access. Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.

It has been revealed that the process starts when a health care provider like a doctor, nurse, or therapist determines that a patient might benefit from a prescription to spend time in nature, including around the nature-inspired visual art at the gallery. The benefits can be many: combating isolation, engaging mentally and physically during a gallery visit, and experiencing awe and beauty.

The prescription to Vancouver Art Gallery includes free admission for the prescription holder and a guest, as well as a printed guide that offers prompts and questions to consider—for example, to notice the varied shades of green Carr used, or imagine a walk along a trail she painted—along with research about the benefits of experiencing nature. Participants are guided through “slow looking” as the act of learning through observation, imagination exercises, and physical movement—yes, swaying in an art gallery is encouraged.

Sources indicate that after the visit, guests are invited to continue the immersion at a local nature space, with free carshare minutes to get there if needed. The art prescription guide suggests nearby parks where participants can walk or hike, extending slow looking from a curated indoor experience to the outdoors if they choose. And they can return to the gallery as often as they like by retaining their original prescription. On site, they can join free workshops, and a coloring book offers a contemplative experience at home.

Recent findings suggest that this is an example of social prescribing, a worldwide movement that serves as a complement to clinical care and typical medication prescriptions by prescribing from a wide range of activities that support physical and mental health. Beyond art galleries and nature walks, this can include music classes, exercise sessions, or gardening programs. The prescription is personal and can be tailored to patients’ needs and interests.

Carla Fry is a West Vancouver psychologist and educator with more than 20 years of clinical experience. She says the art gallery prescription has been a gift for participants, especially those who face physical, mental, social, or even financial or transportation barriers to accessing nature. Many are surprised that they don’t have to pay anything for the experience.

“For them to understand that so many people have come together to create this opportunity, I think that in and of itself is special,” Fry says. “They say, ‘Wow, my community cares.’ The possibility that this exists, it’s available, it’s free—there’s something about that . . . that’s noteworthy.”.

According to recent reports, fry is one of the professionals who gives these kinds of prescriptions to her clients. It’s another tool available to promote well-being.

“Of course, I’m never telling them to go. We talk about this as a prescription, but I always present it as ‘here’s an opportunity to meet some of your goals, and here’s what the opportunity looks like,’” she says.

As yet, no one has declined her prescription.

“They’re surprised that something so seemingly simplistic as slowing down and really looking, really living in front of the art or in nature is actually an intervention,” Fry says. “People in our culture are set up to think that growth has got to be painful, growth has got to be difficult, growth has got to be expensive, growth is going to take a long time. When I bring forward an intervention of going to a location, and your job as a client of mine is to appreciate, the first reaction is surprise. It opens up an entire conversation—‘I can just appreciate my life and not always be grinding to make it better.’ It’s a special process for me to witness.”.

The goal is to do more than increase the number of people who have exposure to art, though that might be a side effect. The formal prescription to nature through art is designed to reduce stress, anxiety, and social isolation. The ability to bring a guest, as well as the opportunity to experience art with other patrons, is key.

Recent findings suggest that “There are other people there; these aren’t private viewings. But of course, sometimes people don’t feel connected to others in a room. Sometimes they do; sometimes it’s enough to feel that they’re part of a community. But others really benefit from being able to have a shared experience where they can reflect in real time and reflect afterwards,” Fry notes.

Paula Toledo is the mental health advisor and lead well-being consultant at Vancouver Art Gallery, leading the Richardson Family Art of Wellbeing Lab. The lab aims to connect the community to art as a means to improve mental and physical well-being, drawing on a collaboration of researchers, scientists, physicians, and Indigenous Elders and healers.

Toledo came to this work through the personal experience of losing her husband and her mother within months, while also caring for her newborn child. That grief and her recovery changed the course of her life and her career in wellness.

“When we encounter something so vast that it transcends our current understanding of the world, it can be very mysterious,” Toledo says:.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes it can be a very positive experience, but other times, like in cases of grief, it can also make you stop and wonder about the mystery behind it. I was in awe and I remember that exact moment where I thought, “Well, if that could happen, then the opposite must also be true.” That’s what the research supports: When we experience awe, it can lead to wonder, which is this mental state of openness and curiosity. Every day I woke up with that sense of curiosity that this might be the day that I turn the corner and collide with good fortune. That experience was so transformative that it led me to actually seek out resources.

Toledo’s health care provider connected her with a social worker who prescribed movement and art in the form of yoga and music classes.

I started to feel more energized and connected to my own self-determination,” she claims. “If we look at the research on why social prescribing is so impactful, it’s because it really does encourage self-determination. I started to feel more connected to my community, more connected to my children, connecting to their own wonder, and it became this upward spiral towards healing and towards rebuilding my life.”.

It has been revealed that monica Harrison is one of the many prescription holders who has learned to lean into the peace and beauty of slowing down through the program. She is an educational assistant who works with students with support needs and advocates for their inclusion in schools. She experienced health issues that required her to be on leave from work and that triggered depression and anxiety.

“I’m neurodivergent, so I’m autistic and I have ADHD. I’ve had anxiety my whole life, and I’ve learned a lot of coping mechanisms that help me to control that. But with undiagnosed conditions that have been going on, it has awoken a lot of anxiety, and it makes it hard to manage my mood,” she says.

According to recent reports, harrison met Toledo, who introduced her to the prescription program. What started with Harrison’s immersion in art has resulted in her increasing use of the program in other locations, both indoors and out.

Sources indicate that harrison, who enjoys nature photography, claims she was introduced to Carr’s paintings in elementary school, and she fell in love with the local subject matter. Now as an adult, that connection to art has opened new opportunities.

“When we visited the gallery, I was able to discuss paintings and identify what I was feeling. It really allowed me to label what I was feeling more accurately and then think about it. Just through her artwork, it really made me feel nurturing and protection,” she notes.

Through other exhibitions at the gallery, Harrison states she found surprise and joy and “a lot of beautiful sensory feelings to my mind and my body and my soul”:.

According to recent reports, chronic illnesses [have] made my life very small, with a lot of losses that come with the territory, such as giving up things that I once enjoyed like working, walking in nature, seeing friends, traveling. I found the prescription to be very flexible. You can do it whenever you’re able to. It can give you something specific to try out. You can do it on your own. You can do it with friends and family, and I think it’s a great thing for people with chronic illness. And it can also give those people a practical way to learn how nature connects to positive mental health. It can be something they can build on through a positive experience with their prescription . . . and add to their toolkit.

Fry says she hears two recurring themes from prescription holders: Experiencing art feels immersive, and the process of visiting the gallery—from the prescription as an invitation to the encouragement to engage in “slow looking”—is a special event that makes them feel cared for.

“It’s something different. It’s something novel. It’s something fresh,” she says, whereas doing the same gratitude practices over and over can get repetitive. “It’s a lot more powerful when we add novel opportunities or events or experiences to our practice. For every person that I’ve prescribed this to, it’s been latest to them, so it hits that mark really nicely,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that art, nature, music, dance, and other social prescriptions have decades of demonstrated success. Toledo points to social prescribing in the U.K. as an example where community connectors or social workers serve as entry points for patients to discover what activities might be meaningful to them. For some, that might mean a return to an activity they enjoyed in years past, like Toledo’s own reengagement with music during her grief.

In a recent development, the social prescription movement continues to gain ground, with providers taking notice at a growing pace. Industry observers note that “In disputes upon moral or scientific points,” Arthur Martine counseled in his magnificent 1866 guide to the art of conversation, “let your aim be to come at truth, not to conquer your opponent. So you never shall be at a loss in losing the argument, and gaining a new discovery.” Of course, this isn’t what happens most of the time when we argue, both online and off, but especially when we deploy the artillery of our righteousness from behind the comfortable shield of the keyboard. That form of “criticism” — which is really a menace of reacting rather than responding — is worthy of Mark Twain’s memorable remark that “the critic’s symbol should be the tumble-bug: he deposits his egg in somebody else’s dung, otherwise he could not hatch it.” But it needn’t be this way — there are ways to be critical while remaining charitable, of aiming not to “conquer” but to “come at truth,” not to be right at all costs but to understand and advance the collective understanding.

Daniel Dennett (March 28, 1942–April 19, 2024), whom artificial intelligence pioneer Marvin Minsky has called “our best current philosopher” and “the next Bertrand Russell,” poses an apt question that probes some of the basic tendencies and dynamics of today’s everyone-is-a-critic culture: “Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crows can make visual decisions twice as rapidly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen.
  • According to recent reports, the findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions.
  • Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crows can make visual decisions twice as rapidly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

According to recent reports, the findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.

Recent findings suggest that to test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.".

Sources indicate that the results showed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds.

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an important role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

Sources indicate that the recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

These signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes.

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," says Andreas Nieder.

Sources indicate that unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as quickly as primates.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially notable for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

In a recent development, however, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

The Only Three Distinctions Between People

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It may be that consciousness evolved to sieve the relevant from the incomprehensible allness of all there is, to parse the world into concepts and find an organizing principle for the chaos of them.
  • Two centuries ago, Nathaniel Hawthorne (July 4, 1804–May 19, 1864) offered a pithy, powerful antidote to this double-edged instinct.
  • In a notebook entry from the autumn of 1836, penned shortly after his moving meditation on how not to waste your life, Hawthorne proposes a revision of our standard classification system for humanity — one that would rehumanize us with the simple awareness that what binds us is infinitely stronger than what divides us or by what affiliations we divide ourselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It may be that consciousness evolved to sieve the relevant from the incomprehensible allness of all there is, to parse the world into concepts and find an organizing principle for the chaos of them. Our cognitive inheritance is a restless yearning to fathom how things cohere and where they belong, a yearning we have given shape to in laws and labels, weights and balances, hierarchies and categories. It has served us well, this instinct to categorize in order to contain, giving us music, the laws of planetary motion, and democracy. But it also pulsates beneath every ism we have ever invented, beneath every stereotype and every genocide, beneath every algorithm that reduces us to variables then adds them up to sell the sum of who we are, beneath all the parcels of preconception we trade daily and mistake the barter a for a genuine encounter with one another.

Two centuries ago, Nathaniel Hawthorne (July 4, 1804–May 19, 1864) offered a pithy, powerful antidote to this double-edged instinct.

In a notebook entry from the autumn of 1836, penned shortly after his moving meditation on how not to waste your life, Hawthorne proposes a revision of our standard classification system for humanity — one that would rehumanize us with the simple awareness that what binds us is infinitely stronger than what divides us or by what affiliations we divide ourselves. He writes:.

A newly introduced classification of society is to be instituted. Instead of rich and poor, high and low, they are to be classed, — First, by their sorrows: for instance, whenever there are any, whether in fair mansion or hovel, who are mourning the loss of relations and friends, and who wear black, whether the cloth be coarse or superfine, they are to make one class. Secondly, all who have the same maladies, whether they lie under damask canopies or on straw pallets or in the wards of hospitals, they are to form one class. Thirdly, all who are guilty of the same sins, whether the world knows them or not; whether they languish in prison, looking forward to the gallows, or walk honored among men, they also form a class. Then proceed to generalize and classify the whole world together, as none can claim utter exemption from either sorrow, sin, or disease; and if they could, yet Death, like a great parent, comes and sweeps all through one darksome portal, — all his children.

What a magnificent way to remember that down where the spirit meets the bone, we are all facing the same struggle: to feel safe, to feel seen, to wrest some meaning and some marvel from the ephemeral bewilderment of being alive.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A smile might brighten your mood, but upcoming research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect.
  • It has been revealed that for years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier.
  • "I used to work in customer service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A smile might brighten your mood, but upcoming research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect. When smiling becomes an obligation, especially one tied to financial pressure, it may actually leave people feeling less happy and more irritated.

It has been revealed that for years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier. Yet those findings never quite matched his own experiences.

"I used to work in customer service. I actually got written up for my inability to keep smiling at work at an unnamed theme park in Florida," laughed Coles, a professor of psychology at the University of Florida. "So I'm looking at all this evidence I had accrued so far that smiling boosts happiness and realizing it flies in the face of my own experiences in the world.".

That contradiction inspired Coles and his colleagues to investigate what happens when people must keep smiling, rather than simply trying it once. Their findings suggest an notable distinction: A brief, intentional smile can provide a small emotional lift, but repeatedly putting on a smile under pressure can undermine happiness.

Testing How Forced Smiling Affects Happiness.

According to recent reports, to explore this difference, Coles worked with researchers Annabel Dang and Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi to design an experiment that more closely resembled the demands of customer service jobs. Their findings were published on October 1 in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

In a recent development, "We tried to combine the classic way of studying it in a lab with some extra ingredients that we might see in the real world. We told participants that we would pay them less if they weren't successfully smiling," Coles said. "We also controlled the number of times they have to do it, because in customer service, every interaction is another faked smile.".

Sources indicate that the online experiment initially enrolled 1,201 people, with data from 1,174 included in the final analysis. Participants were shown images designed to produce different emotional reactions. Some depicted appealing subjects, such as kittens and flowers, while others showed disturbing situations, including theft and mistreatment of animals.

It has been revealed that during the experiment, participants either deliberately formed a smile or allowed their facial expressions to develop naturally. Depending on their assigned group, they completed the exercise once or repeated it 10 times.

Recent findings suggest that to introduce an element of pressure, researchers warned half the participants that failing to follow the smiling instructions could cost them $2 from their $6 payment. However, nobody actually lost any money, and every participant received the full amount.

When Fake Smiles Start to Backfire.

Industry observers note that after completing each task, participants reported how happy they felt. The results showed that the emotional effects of smiling depended on how often people had to do it and whether they felt pressured.

Industry observers note that when participants viewed unpleasant images, producing a single smile gave their mood a modest boost. This benefit appeared even among those who had been warned about a possible financial penalty. However, the positive effect weakened when smiling was repeated, and it disappeared when repeated smiles were combined with the threat of losing money.

In a recent development, the pattern was even more revealing when people looked at pleasant pictures. Smiling just once offered little additional happiness compared with allowing their faces to respond naturally. But when participants had to smile repeatedly or felt pressure to do so, their happiness ratings actually fell below those of people who responded naturally.

Further analysis revealed another unexpected consequence. In the pleasant picture conditions, forced smiling was also associated with increased irritation and anger.

Sources indicate that "If you only force a smile once without any financial penalties, you can see the improvement in happiness. So what psychologists were seeing in their lab is right," he stated. "But when you make it a little bit more like the real world, where you have to keep repeating it, and if you don't do it well, you get financial penalties, you see it completely reverse.".

The Hidden Emotional Cost of Smiling at Work.

These findings may help explain why expectations to appear cheerful throughout the workday can become frustrating rather than uplifting.

According to recent reports, the problem has already sparked controversy in the workplace. In recent years, Target faced widespread criticism over a policy requiring employees to smile when customers came within a specified distance. Although the policy was intended to encourage friendly interactions, Coles argues that such requirements can interfere with people's ability to express their emotions naturally.

Industry observers note that the problem may extend beyond employees. Customers can also feel obligated to respond positively to friendliness that is being imposed rather than offered spontaneously. According to Coles, these expectations limit the emotional freedom of both sides of the interaction.

Could Trying Less to Be Happy Make Us Happier?

After spending years investigating how people can improve their emotional well-being, Coles has begun considering a broader question. Rather than constantly searching for ways to increase happiness, might people be better off placing greater value on simply being content?

His research suggests that efforts to manufacture positive emotions do not always produce the intended results. Sometimes, trying too hard to appear happy can make the experience less pleasant.

"As a society, we have placed such an immense amount of emphasis on trying to make ourselves feel happier than we at the moment are," he stated, "much less emphasis on just being content with what we have.".

#206400. US affordable artists' housing initiatives hobbled by uneven regulation and oversight

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2256 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

US affordable artists' housing initiatives hobbled by uneven regulation and oversight

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, “Affordability” is on the lips of every American.
  • National non-profits such as Artspace and the Community Arts Stabilization Trust (Cast) arrived in the state recently, participating in the many funding programmes supporting this effort.
  • In a recent development, “We were floored,” artists Emilie Dundee Odeile and Ken Lee Chapin tell The Art Newspaper, when their work Goodnight Moon: A Fiber Tale drew more than 10,000 visitors to Trinidad, a town of 8,000 people near Colorado’s southern border.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “Affordability” is on the lips of every American. In Colorado, over 35% of residents spend more than 30% of their income on housing, which is considered a cost burden by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (Hud). The state is responding by allocating $300m annually to the State Affordable Housing Fund. A niche area of this investment is the development of affordable housing for artists and creative districts.

National non-profits such as Artspace and the Community Arts Stabilization Trust (Cast) arrived in the state recently, participating in the many funding programmes supporting this effort. Both non-profits market affordable housing for artists, but in the absence of artist certification programmes such as those in Boston, Newly introduced York and now San Francisco, restricting available affordable housing to artists could run the risk of violating fair housing laws. There are also few mechanisms for cities and states to ensure their public funding delivers long-term solutions for artists’ housing and creative spaces.

In a recent development, “We were floored,” artists Emilie Dundee Odeile and Ken Lee Chapin tell The Art Newspaper, when their work Goodnight Moon: A Fiber Tale drew more than 10,000 visitors to Trinidad, a town of 8,000 people near Colorado’s southern border. The artists used around 152 miles of yarn to bring the famous children’s book to life in a 2023 exhibition.

“We started our RV-life, one-year road trip experiment,” Chapin states. “We were on our way to Santa Fe, and went through Trinidad”—and they never left. Goodnight Moon and another project by Odeile debuted at Space to Create, a state-led initiative to produce creative workforce housing and studios in rural Colorado.

Trinidad was the first municipality identified by the Colorado Office of Economic Development and International Trade (OEDIT) for public investment through the establishment of a creative district, in 2015. Today, 37 creative districts exist across the state. Next door to Space to Create on Trinidad’s historic Main Street, Artspace manages residences for artists.

In a recent development, artspace develops and operates workforce housing across 23 states, including seven projects in Colorado. Each project markets itself “for those in the creative sector” and offers residential space that “prioritises creative use”. But without a formal certification programme to identify artists in Colorado or any of the local municipalities it operates in, it is unclear how Artspace can legally give preference to artist applicants over members of the general public.

Poet and editor Michele McDannold lived in Artspace’s complex in Michigan City, Indiana, for nearly four years and at the organisation’s Honolulu location for seven months. She arrived in Trinidad in 2020, but noticed a substantial difference in the artist preference process at that location compared to the properties she had been in previously. In Michigan City, she notes, “I had to give a presentation to a board of practicing artists and participate in an interview.” In Trinidad, she was only asked to submit information for income eligibility. McDannold has only encountered five artists across the property’s 40 units during her three-year stay. The result of not prioritising artist applicants appeared to be that there were almost no artist residents.

“When it came time to organise or participate in something like [open studios or a gallery night],” McDannold claims, “neighbours were like, ‘What? Why are you bothering me?”.

Artspace did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s multiple requests for comment. The Artspace Trinidad leasing office stated that it does not track the number of artist residents at that location.

Affordable housing is a broad term that lives on a spectrum of interpretation and regulation. According to the federal government, household affordability is based on the regional or area median income (AMI). What a property owner can charge a tenant is determined by Hud’s AMI calculations, but a lender can set the contractual terms of the tax credit, loan or grant, whether private or public. Under US Treasury regulations, a housing unit generates a low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC) only if it is available for general-public use. However, in 2008 the Housing and Economic Recovery Act added a provision to the Internal Revenue Service’s tax code stating that general-public use is not violated if preference is given to tenants involved in artistic or literary activities. Even so, some cities maintain their own artist certification programmes for affordable housing.

Recent findings suggest that A 2023 affordable housing audit by Denver’s Department of Housing Stability expressed concerns that priority access to housing could violate the federal Fair Housing Act. While the report specifically focused on the Denver city council’s move to prioritise displaced households or people at risk of displacement, it highlighted the fact that prioritising seniors and veterans also requires better systems for monitoring and evaluation. Each time a person, such as an artist, is prioritised for affordable housing access, the county must track data such as the number of units allocated, eligibility requirements, types of document accepted as evidence of eligibility, the selection process, and the parties responsible for implementation and monitoring the property and rent levels.

Industry observers note that municipal governments are concerned about incurring fair housing lawsuits, especially if state and county laws contradict or fail to reaffirm the 2008 tax code revision. Cities considering allocating affordable housing units for artists can be faced with having to develop significant compliance procedures. This patchwork of rules, requirements and compliance regimes helps explain why creating and maintaining affordable housing for artists can be very complicated, costly, and look different in different cities and regions. According to the Center for an Urban Future, US cities have created just 2,804 units of dedicated housing for artists in the last decade.

Recent findings suggest that the soaring windows of 210 East Street in Trinidad must have caught the eye of the developer Dana Crawford when she first visited the elegant century-old school building. Crawford, who died in January 2025, was a celebrated preservationist in the region, known for saving Denver’s historic Larimer Square and redeveloping the city’s Union Station. There were minimal requirements attached to the $4m community revitalisation grant Crawford received for the redevelopment of 210 East Street into 17 affordable live-work spaces for artists. An open records request reveals the terms of the grant for the property only ask for progress reports on the number of housing units and jobs created.

The Former East Street School building in Trinidad, Colorado has been converted to housing and marketed as affordable for artists, among others Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust.

According to recent reports, for the 210 East Street project, Crawford procured three different tax credits, the $4m community revitalisation grant and $1.8m in private financing, but the most restrictive terms were attached to last-minute funding from the city of Trinidad. In 2022 Crawford applied to the city’s Housing Now incentive programme to help cover the $125,000 cost of redesigning five units. The city approved the request on the condition of a two-year workforce housing deed restriction, requiring rent rates to be limited to 80% of AMI starting in 2023.

In a recent development, crawford also sought $1.9m in funding from an impact investor, Greenland CDF. The funding from Greenland was contingent on signing a Community Benefit Agreement (CBA), a binding contract that requires the borrower to produce a social benefit with enforceable penalties. The details of the agreement are not public and expired earlier this year.

Recent findings suggest that less than five years after Crawford received a total of $7.5m in public funding for 210 East Street, the property was acquired by Cast. There are no existing public terms that legally require Cast to deliver affordable housing to artists, or even general housing.

Cast operates a non-profit real estate development strategy around creative spaces and affordability. Recently, the organisation expanded that strategy to housing in Colorado.

“Our model as a non-profit is to reset the floor of affordability,” says Ken Ikeda, Cast’s chief executive. “If we could do that without debt, through grants, then that would keep it that way in perpetuity.”.

Right now, Ikeda adds, Cast is only required to deliver the private terms of the $1.9m grant the organisation received from the Colorado Health Foundation to acquire 210 East Street. Rent at the complex is currently between 55% and 80% of AMI, and according to a spokesperson for the organisation, five current residents are artists. The Art Newspaper was only able to verify that one resident is an artist, and that person mentioned they know of no others.

Half a mile from 210 East Street are three properties that have received significant public funding in exchange for affordable artists’ housing. In 2019 ownership of two addresses on Main Street and one on Elm Street were transferred to Artspace by the city of Trinidad. In exchange for that real estate and a $715,000 promissory note by the Colorado Housing Finance Authority in 2022, Artspace must deliver housing units within or below 40% to 60% of AMI for 35 years, and preserve the historic facade of the Main Street properties for 15 years. If it fails to maintain this commitment, it must repay the borrowed funds.

The vastly different requirements for the Artspace and Cast properties in Trinidad, and the strings attached (or not) to their public and private funding reflect the wildly different standards and requirements for organisations creating and operating affordable artists’ housing.

The 444 17th Street building in Denver, the future site of a multi-use affordable housing and cultural hub for artists, to be operated by Community Arts Stabilization Trust Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust.

In a recent development, A vibrant art and culture scene boosts local businesses and helps create jobs, according to the Denver Downtown Development Authority (DDDA), a city initiative to revive a downtown core where the vacancy rate has remained at or above 30% since the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2025 and 2026 the DDDA awarded $114.5m in financing for new housing and $4.45m for art-related initiatives—including a $1.35m grant to Cast to convert 6,300 sq. ft of vacant office and retail space into affordable artists’ studios, a cinema and gallery. The city council approved the terms of the property’s sale to Cast in September.

It has been revealed that “We are going to make it affordable no matter what, because that is our aim and objective,” Ikeda claims of the project in Denver, which has been vacant since 2021. Cast estimates the art space will open in the summer of 2027.

Representatives for the city did not clarify how it defines “affordable” in the context of commercial real estate, but noted that the city has the first right to purchase the property for $1 for the next ten years if Cast decides to sell. In the meantime, municipal support will be released in phases as Cast reaches a series of build-out milestones.

It has been revealed that while Denver finds its footing on affordable housing for artists and New York has not added any units in a decade, San Francisco’s first dedicated affordable artists’ housing is on track to open in 2028. The Artist Hub on Market, at 1687 Market Street, will have 94 units of housing, rehearsal space and a theatre. Rent will be set between 30% and 80% of the AMI, depending on the size of the unit and number of occupants, which equates to annual income of between $46,440 and $167,120 for tenants.

A rendering of the future Artists Hub on Market project in San Francisco Courtesy Artists Hub on Market and Mercy Housing California.

In a recent development, launching alongside the Market Street property is a upcoming artist certification programme for San Francisco, facilitated by the Mayor’s Office of Housing and Community Development. Artists can achieve certification by documenting at least $10,000 in annual income from their art practice, showing proof of a public art commission or grant in the previous three years, or submitting a portfolio of work for review. Once certification is awarded, artists can enter the lottery for units at Artist Hub on Market; any units unclaimed by artists in the lottery will be opened to general-public use through the city’s affordable housing system.

Of the Artist Hub on Market project’s $140m in funding, $100m came from a single anonymous donor and, according to a source familiar with the terms of the deal, implementing the artist certification programme was a condition of the funding.

The inconsistent regulation of properties that receive public funding for affordable artists’ housing and cultural spaces risks undermining such projects’ longevity and disappointing the communities they were meant to serve. Recently, a $400,000 low-interest loan from the DDDA to Denver Immersive Repertory Theater (Dirt) went into default after Dirt’s alleged failure to make rent payments less than a year after it was awarded the loan and before its project ever opened to the public. According to reporting by Denverite, the loan’s rate surges from 3% to 15% when loan proceeds are shown to not be used for their intended purpose, though it is unclear what assets the city will be able to claw back from the project’s founders.

According to recent reports, affordable housing for artists is an emerging sector entangled with various local governments’ goals, which include attracting business, lowering housing costs by adding units and retaining creative workers. Ikeda describes every affordability project as a funding “butterfly” due to the unique risks and complexity of the capital and terms assembled. But, he adds, they are worth the trouble: “There is something magical about artist-only housing and live-work environments.”.

#206399. Designing For Distressed Owners: Why Mental Health Apps Shouldn’t Follow Every UI Fashion

📅 2026-07-09 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3557 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Designing For Distressed Owners: Why Mental Health Apps Shouldn’t Follow Every UI Fashion

📅 2026-07-09 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that kat Homan is a product (UX/UI) designer at DŌBRA Studio.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Mental health applications keep facing a continuing, measurable crisis: many people stop using them quickly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that kat Homan is a product (UX/UI) designer at DŌBRA Studio. She designs B2C mobile and web products, including four mental-health products and have prior … More about Kat ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Mental health applications keep facing a continuing, measurable crisis: many people stop using them quickly. The data is stark: almost 95% of customers who open the app on day 1 abandon the app by day 30, with a median 30-day retention of only 3.3%. Even the recognised mental health giants lose around 50% of their users within the first ten days. This severe engagement loss and retention collapse are why effective interface design must be a clinical and operational priority. Good design is not merely aesthetic; it is a fundamental tool for user retention.

Recent findings suggest that while many factors drive this abandonment, research suggests that mental health apps have tended to prioritise visual appeal at the expense of what actually sustains consumers. In a space defined by vulnerability and cognitive strain, chasing visual fashion risks adding effort when users have the least to spare — quietly trading away the utility and trust the app depends on. Users don’t open mental health apps out of curiosity, but from need — often while stressed, anxious, overwhelmed, or exhausted. In these states, an unconventional icon, a confusing gesture, or a flashy animation instead of a delightful surprise becomes an extra cognitive overload. Moreover, it becomes a reason to disengage.

Industry observers note that in those moments, visual experimentation from a mild distraction can turn into a friction that undermines the very help the app is meant to deliver. A solution must be a visual interface that is simple in usage and understanding from the first moment.

Crucially, improving engagement depends less on which UI trends you follow than on a single test applied to each one of them: does a trend lower the cost of using the app when the user can least afford it?

Before we look into the specific problems, we must recognise a core tension: many UI trends are optimised for goals that mental health apps don’t share.

Pursuing the former directly overrides the latter. It’s not a surface-level error of colour or font; it’s a foundational conflict of purpose. This tension surfaces across five fronts, each a place where adopting a trend on novelty alone can cost more engagement than it seeks to create.

Sources indicate that the proposed principles are not based on a single A/B test or one isolated study. They are built from published research on mental health app engagement, cognitive load, accessibility, and emotional response in mHealth, set against competitive product audits and app-store evidence, and pressure-tested against my own quantitative and qualitative product work. That last source I treat as an illustration, understanding the limits of personal experience. In this context, validation is less about proving that one interface pattern universally works and more about asking whether a design reduces effort, preserves agency, avoids emotional mismatch, and remains usable when the user is already under strain.

In a recent development, A note on the examples: This isn’t a ranking of apps. Every app has its own positioning, target audience, constraints, and business pressures that may not be visible from outside, and a pattern that strains a user in distress may be exactly right for that product’s actual goal. I’m reading individual, visible design decisions for one question only: how they might affect someone arriving in a low-capacity state.

Recent findings suggest that the primary goal of any mental health tool is to reduce, not increase, cognitive load. Yet, many trendy interfaces achieve the opposite. Neo-brutalist layouts with stark contrasts demand visual parsing. Hidden navigation menus that rely on non-standard swipes turn simple tasks into puzzles. Abstract, unlabeled icons force consumers to guess rather than recognise. Each of these patterns adds friction — seconds of hesitation, a moment of confusion — and for a user whose mental energy is already low, those costs start to accumulate.

This friction is most damaging during acute need. Research suggests that when a user is in a state of high anxiety or depression, even typing or making simple choices can feel overwhelming. When an interface demands high cognitive effort at the moment support is needed, it doesn’t just make that session harder — it gives an overwhelmed user a reason to close the app, and a reason not to reopen it. Each point of confusion can become a place where a user may quit for good.

Industry observers note that other findings show that apps with simple interfaces reduce the time and effort required to engage, directly improving retention. Conversely, a complex, trend-driven UI increases that time, creating an obstacle course that undermines the very healthy habit formation the app is meant to support.

Recent findings suggest that this does not mean that every mental health product must be visually plain or minimal. The issue is whether the interface meets the user’s current capacity.

A panic-support tool, for example, works best when it offers a small number of obvious actions, rather than asking the user to browse. However, if a calming action meant for a moment of panic instead surfaces an upgrade screen, the product fails the user at precisely the point where failing matters most. Monetization is not the concern by itself; the issue is whether it appears at a point where the user expects immediate support.

Nonori demonstrates the same principle in a more reflective context. The app does not present the user with a large content library or a complex dashboard at the start. Instead, it leads them through a simple, linear sequence of small actions. The value of this pattern is that it reduces the effort needed to begin. When a user is tired, anxious, or mentally overloaded, knowing exactly what to do next can lower the barrier to returning.

Industry observers note that at the other end of the spectrum, comprehensive tracking apps show a different trade-off. Bearable, for example, is genuinely powerful: it consolidates almost everything a person tracks — mood, symptoms, sleep, medication, habits, reports, correlations — into one place. For people managing chronic conditions or preparing for medical appointments, this can be genuinely useful. But the same comprehensiveness can become a burden for an exhausted user. Dense dashboards and multi-step check-ins require executive capacity — the very resource that anxiety, depression, burnout, or brain fog often reduce.

Recent findings suggest that A similar tension appears in anxiety apps with strong support content but busy entry points. A product may contain useful features yet still make the first screen feel noisy with too many cards, locked items, playful characters, or upgrade prompts. This is not evidence that the product is bad. It shows how the same interface can feel very different depending on the user’s state: clear enough during exploration, but too demanding during distress.

This insight shaped a guiding principle for our work: every interaction point must meet owners at their current level of capacity, removing mechanical and cognitive barriers rather than adding to them. This principle guided our integration of low-friction, state-aware interactions in apps like Bear Room, a stress and anxiety reduction app, and Teeni, an emotional-wellbeing app for parents of teens.

In Bear Room, we already had a fast mood-based flow built around four emotion cards. At the same time, our product research supported a second need: consumers also wanted more personalised support. We avoided making this a long selection flow or a typing-only route because both can still create friction for people under stress or anxiety. Instead, we made voice a primary, prominent path, always alongside a text alternative. A central microphone button allows users to share what’s on their mind. The app then uses AI to analyse the input and provide a tailored set of coping practices.

Industry observers note that rather than picking a single entry model, we kept two paths because they served different states. That matched what we saw in later analytics and user conversations: quick emotional selection worked better when users wanted speed, while open voice or text input worked better when they wanted personalisation and to feel more heard. This was more a pattern we noticed, without having the exact measured results.

Similarly, in Teeni, we directly addressed the cognitive friction of parenting stress by introducing a “Quick Relief” button. This creates an empathy-friendly flow for parents experiencing anger or frustration. The button initiates a dedicated “Hot Flow,” allowing them to first vent and relieve their immediate negative emotions through voice input. Only after this emotional release does the app gently guide them into the more reflective “Cold Flow” for the rest of the app’s resources. This sequential, state-sensitive design acknowledges that a user in peak distress cannot navigate a complex app; they need a direct, simple, and validating first step.

These solutions directly tackle cognitive friction by meeting consumers at their level of capacity, resisting trends that add visual or interaction complexity. Voice input and single-action buttons remove the mechanical and cognitive burden of navigation and typing. The result is an interface that feels reliably non-judgmental and genuinely helpful when users are least equipped to navigate complexity.

A user’s emotional state is the context in which a mental health app operates. This is why its visual language must be empathetic and considerate. Research investigating how colour and aesthetics influence mood in mHealth apps suggests a critical insight: people in distress show a strong preference for subtlety. They long for dark palettes, sleek and sophisticated looks, and clean, uncluttered aesthetics, explicitly noting that cheerful, bright colours, while seemingly appropriate, can create a jarring, even physically uncomfortable conflict with their current mood.

In a recent development, this does not mean that every mental health or wellbeing app should look dark, quiet, or clinically restrained. The category is broad: it includes self-care, anxiety support, habit change, addiction recovery, trauma tools, therapy-adjacent products, and apps for more severe mental health contexts. A playful visual style may be appropriate for one product and a poor fit for another. What matters is not whether the interface is bright or muted, but whether its emotional tone fits the product’s purpose and the likely state in which customers arrive.

Sources indicate that emotional mismatch can also appear in mechanics, not only in aesthetics. In Calmer, an anxiety and panic relief app, the interface itself appeared relatively clean and relaxed. Yet some of its engagement and monetisation mechanics sit in a different register from that relaxed: a discount wheel, or confetti celebrating a logged low mood. For a user who just recorded a hard moment, that shift — from quiet support to upsell or celebration — can land as a mismatch, whatever its intent.

For Bear Room, we prototyped a “cosy room” design informed by direct feedback from our users, which echoed the study’s conclusions. Several users in our research described the apps they had tried for similar needs as “too bright, too happy, and too overwhelming”. Users longed for a digital safe space. This was part of what pointed us toward a quieter palette in the final design: muted, earthy tones — neutral hues like soft greens and taupes — set against darker, calming backgrounds. For this product — a refuge for users arriving overwhelmed — that meant a middle ground: a space that feels safe without being gloomy. The interface avoided any bright alerts or sudden animations, making calmness the core feature.

This case underscores a critical principle: an overly cheerful, bold, or trend-forward interface can feel dismissive to someone in distress, creating a conflict that erodes trust. As Bear Room reveals, trust is built when the interface respectfully aligns with the user’s emotional reality, offering solace through subtlety (which creates an overall feeling of a “welcoming and safe atmosphere”), not a solution through saturation.

Industry observers note that mental health often relies on routine and predictability. Yet many contemporary UI trends thrive on novelty and disruption, intentionally reimagining fundamental navigation. When an app introduces a novel interaction pattern, such as a unique swipe or a non-standard button behavior, it asks the user to learn something before they can act, forcing them into cognitive effort they can’t afford.

Sources indicate that this does not mean that mental health apps must be plain, rigid, or generic. A product can have its own character, playfulness, and sense of identity. The question is whether that identity remains understandable and predictable when the user returns in a low-capacity state. A gamified self-care app like Finch may work well when the user arrives ready to explore, play, and build a routine. But open it after a hard day just to mark one task done, and the can’t-skip celebration screens that delight an engaged user become one more layer to get through before they reach what they came for.

Industry observers note that A similar tension appears in large meditation and wellbeing platforms. Apps such as Headspace and Calm offer extensive libraries of different content. This breadth can be valuable during exploration. But in moments of stress, the product question becomes sharper: can the user return and immediately find the exact support they need, or do they have to search, filter, and relearn the structure?

Someone experiencing anxiety or executive dysfunction needs to use the tool in a straightforward navigation manner, not an interface they have to learn each time anew.

PTSD Coach, a public-health-oriented trauma-support app designed to help consumers learn about and manage symptoms after trauma, offers a useful positive example. Its interface is not trying to be fashion-forward. Its strength lies in a stable information architecture: users can learn, track symptoms, manage symptoms, and get support through clearly separated areas. For a user returning during distress, this predictability matters more than novelty.

CALMzone offers another useful example. Some of its breathing animations differ from standard visual patterns, but they remain tied to the exercise itself: the animation shows what to do, when to inhale, and when to hold. The guided audio screen also explicitly invites the user to put the phone down and listen. This is a rare and valuable form of interaction design: the product’s success is not more screen time, but reduced effort and regulation.

These insights guided our approach in applications like Bear Room, where navigation reliability was treated as a therapeutic feature. We intentionally crafted an experience of an empathetic guided flow.

Recent findings suggest that recognising that customers would likely approach in states of overwhelm, we structured the interface as a clear, unwavering path, with a visible “Start” sign. Key emotional support tools here are represented as the room’s objects — symbols of daily life, unmistakably recognised by all. They are visually highlighted by design so that the user won’t get lost in the elements, can easily access the needed tool, and can remember their way around the digital space upon the next return to the app.

Trend-driven interfaces sacrifice this navigational certainty for novelty. Each unconventional choice in mHealth apps, when core functions are buried behind experimental interactions or placed in unexpected locations, leads to a cumulative effect of fatigue instead of innovation. Owners are not in a place to explore. They abandon the entire practice of seeking digital support when every interaction feels like solving a fresh puzzle. This does not restrict experimentation; it simply means that animations, micro-interactions, AI, or playful mechanics must serve the user’s state rather than interrupt it.

In a recent development, many popular UI trends can be exclusionary when applied without adaptation. The minimalist trend of low-contrast text fails people with visual impairments. Gesture-only navigation marginalises those with motor difficulties. Visually dense, animated interfaces can overwhelm users with cognitive or attentional conditions. In mental health, the population needing support disproportionately includes individuals with these accessibility needs.

Recent findings suggest that choosing a trending aesthetic over an accessible one is therefore an active decision to limit the app’s reach and efficacy. It ensures that those who might benefit most cannot use the tool effectively. Accessibility isn’t a layer you add at the end; it’s a constraint you design within, with most of it codified in Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2. Body text needs 4.5:1 contrast against its background, large text and interface elements 3:1 — exactly what low-contrast minimalism fails. Interactive targets need a floor of 24×24 px (more for unsteady hands). Every gesture needs a visible button fallback, or you risk excluding anyone who can’t perform the swipe.

In a recent development, A final, and often overlooked, consequence of trend-following is the adoption of engagement mechanics designed for entertainment, educational, or productivity apps. Features like streaks, aggressive notifications, and gamified reward systems are engineered to maximise screen time and create dependency. Although they have long been considered effective tools for increasing retention, in a mental health context, this approach can easily be misguided. What presents as “motivation” can swiftly transform into a source of performance pressure and guilt. For a user managing depression, a broken streak or a missed daily goal can exacerbate the very feelings the app aims to alleviate.

These mechanics are not inherently unethical. In routine-building products, they can help some owners. The risk appears when they are transferred into mental health contexts without adapting for shame, low energy, relapse, and non-linear recovery. A streak, for example, is not just a retention mechanic when the user is emotionally vulnerable. It can become a visible record of whether they have “kept up” with their well-being.

In the apps I reviewed, this tension appeared through familiar persuasion patterns: streaks, streak freezes, commitment copy, urgency-based notifications, “don’t miss this offer” prompts, and success-framed buttons such as “Yes, I want to succeed.” In self-care or wellbeing products, these details can make the app feel less like a supportive tool and more like another system the user has to satisfy.

Industry observers note that designers still need return triggers. A mental health app has little value if users install it once and forget it exists. But return mechanics must be adapted to the emotional context. In Bear Room, for example, this philosophy is embodied in short, forgiving three-day streaks: the streak does not reset when a user misses a day, and every third day brings a small benefit. The goal is not to punish absence, but to gently support return.

Sources indicate that the same principle applies to lighter interactions. Bear Room includes a simple, optional bubble-popping game. Its purpose, however, is not to hook the user but to offer a brief, calming interlude. It is deliberately finite, providing a small mood lift and gently signposting other resources within the app. The value is in the momentary relief, not the extended session.

This commitment to supportive, non-coercive design extends to foundational app architecture:.

In mental health technology, sustainable retention is earned not by capturing attention, but by becoming a consistently respectful and helpful presence in a user’s life.

The mHealth apps design invites finding a challenging balance between boosting their use without being too demanding.

According to recent reports, this is not a niche concern affecting a fringe audience. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that about one billion people globally live with a mental disorder, with depression alone affecting nearly 5% of adults. Critically, the overall number is rising — in the last decade, depression and anxiety cases have increased by 25%. This vast and vulnerable population cannot afford for its tools to fail due to poor design. While UI trends aren’t inherently problematic, their application within wellbeing products demands a radically contextual approach.

It has been revealed that even a five-minute decompression tool between meetings has an emotional context, and a style chosen for its look — glassmorphism, a certain flavour of ultra-minimalism — can miss it, however sophisticated the audience. The point isn’t that these styles are wrong; it’s that the look has to answer to the moment. Soft biomorphic shapes or fluid transitions can genuinely help when they directly serve the goal of calm — and the same elements become noise when they’re there to impress.

The five fronts outlined above are not just a diagnostic lens; they are the foundation of an evaluation framework for anyone designing in the mental health space. Before incorporating any trendy visual or interaction pattern, it is worth running it through each of them in sequence:.

A design that passes all five holds together as something more than usable: it becomes a tool that owners can trust enough to return to in moments of genuine need.

Trends can be inspiring. They can win awards and generate buzz. But in mental health, sometimes the best design is the one that helps users feel understood — a quiet helper they trust enough to return to in moments of stress and vulnerability. It doesn’t steal the spotlight, but focuses on the user’s emotions. In the end, the ultimate goal is not for the interface to be seen — but for the support to be felt.

The Most Powerful Attitude You Can Take Toward Your Life and the Life of the World

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, perhaps the gravest violence we can do to ourselves is to live out our lives believing the world to be a fixity handed down to us by the authorities of history and life to be a matter of taking immutable givens.
  • James Baldwin knew this when he issued his lyrical and impassioned insistence that “nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed,” that “we made the world we’re living in and we have to make it over.”.
  • Hannah Arendt knew this when she considered how we invent ourselves and reinvent the world, observing that “the smallest act in the most limited circumstances bears the seed of boundlessness, because one deed, and sometimes one word, suffices to change every constellation.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, perhaps the gravest violence we can do to ourselves is to live out our lives believing the world to be a fixity handed down to us by the authorities of history and life to be a matter of taking immutable givens. Daring to believe otherwise — to believe that even our smallest purposeful action alters the monolith of reality in some subtle, meaningful way — is an act of courage and resistance, an act of immense vulnerability to the possibility of disappointment, vulnerability the commonest cowering from which is cynicism.

James Baldwin knew this when he issued his lyrical and impassioned insistence that “nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed,” that “we made the world we’re living in and we have to make it over.”.

Hannah Arendt knew this when she considered how we invent ourselves and reinvent the world, observing that “the smallest act in the most limited circumstances bears the seed of boundlessness, because one deed, and sometimes one word, suffices to change every constellation.”.

It has been revealed that richard Powers knew this when he made his contribution to Take My Advice: Letters to the Next Generation from People Who Know a Thing or Two (public library) — artist and writer James L. Harmon’s wonderful 2002 anthology of wisdom from stellar minds, a decade in the constellating, envisioned as an eclectic contemporary counterpart to Rilke’s timeless Letters to a Young Poet, which had moved Harmon deeply when he first encountered it as a young man.

Two decades before Powers won the Pulitzer Prize for his sylvan symphony The Overstory, he echoes Seamus Heaney’s exhortation to always remain “true to your own secret knowledge” and writes:.

In a recent development, never forget what you were born knowing. That this fluke, single, huge, cross-indexed, thermodynamic experiment of a story that the world has been inventing to tell itself at bedtime is still in embryo. It’s not even the outline of a synopsis of notes toward a rough draft yet. Buy the plot some time.

It has been revealed that we buy the plot time with the currency of our conscious choices, the grand and the mundane alike — the daily actions that make us what we are, the people who make the world what it is. Powers writes:.

Take in more, consume less, recycle everything; book-keep all hidden costs; find out where you have been set down; lobby for a smaller market; get rid of your car and travel as widely as you can (yeah, walk: what the hell); try to say a little more than you mean; carry a pocket encyclopedia (ask for one without packaging) and when the entry on “Diffusion Constant” says, “for more information, see ‘Pastry War,'” see “Pastry War.”.

It has been revealed that this latter sentiment might at first appear dated in the hindsight of two decades, in the epoch of Wikipedia. But it is actually all the more insightful and urgent today, for the quiet act of resistance at its heart has grown all the harder. What I most rue about the internet is that, for all its riches of readily accessible information, it has altered the texture of human curiosity, vanquishing that wondrous encyclopedic feeling of learning about the thing you hadn’t known you didn’t know but now greatly enjoy knowing. Somewhere along the way of choices being made for us by an insular tribe of technologists, discovery was sacrificed at the altar of search as algorithms perfected the mechanics of giving us more and more of what we already knew we wanted and believed, rendering the mind itself more and more a fixity. Would you be Googling “Pastry War” now had I not made this point about a point Richard Powers made long ago on the pages of a yellowing book I pulled from my bookshelf by some incomputable human impulse this morning?

Those choices matter, Powers reminds us, even at the smallest scale. There is no fulcrum too small for the lever of change to lift from, but the lift must begin with lucidity. He writes:.

In a recent development, take a full look at the worst. Acknowledge the figures: the runaway birthdates, the irreversible extinctions and ruined habitats, the meaningless economies fueled by waste, the exported shooting wars and their cover causes… Then work at whatever comes to hand. Useful or not, it makes no difference. Jumping in is the only calculus that emergency ever allows.

Complement with Rebecca Solnit on rewriting the world’s broken stories with our actions, then revisit What If — a wondrous French picture-book about daring to imagine and build a different world for the children of tomorrow.

#206397. Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize.
  • Industry observers note that the findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an crucial role in physical and mental well-being.
  • In a recent development, the discovery could be especially notable for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

Industry observers note that the findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an crucial role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

In a recent development, the discovery could be especially notable for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression.

Industry observers note that to investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

In a recent development, as researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

Recent findings suggest that participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

According to recent reports, "Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy stated. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes.".

Why Your Body's Internal Clock Matters.

Sources indicate that one possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Industry observers note that rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially notable, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

When these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy said.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

The Hidden Effects of Social Jet Lag.

Even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

Industry observers note that someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

It has been revealed that "As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy remarked. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake.".

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits.

The research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains important, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.
