📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design. After more than a decade of working in tech, he … More about Brecht ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment. But when I heard that the native CSS random() function landed in Safari and is rolling out in Chrome 156, I started wondering: where does randomness actually make sense on the web? Is it something we want in our design system? To find out, I did what I always do in doubt: I built a bunch of playful CodePen demos exploring organic typography, bouncing letters, splayed cards, and a punk fanzine.

In a recent development, as someone who loves building design systems and tinkering with CSS architecture, a major part of my day job revolves around control. We set up spacing scales, lock down typography, set up color tokens, and make sure everything aligns on a grid. Consistency is usually our bread and butter as design engineers and a proud badge of skill when creating design systems. If a card suddenly jumps 20 pixels to the left on a refresh, it’s not creative expression; it’s a bug that the project manager will log.

So when I first heard that the native random() function from the CSS Values and Units Level 5 spec was shipped in Safari, and is right now rolling out in Chrome 156 (with positive signals from Mozilla on Firefox as well), my first reaction was: that’s pretty cool!

And my second reaction was: wait… where would I actually use this without making a mess? How can I convince designers that random might be a good idea for a design system?

Sources indicate that because let’s be honest: why on earth would we want randomness in our stylesheets when we’ve spent the last decade trying to make the web more predictable? Even when using flexbox or fluid typography, we’re still trying to make things as aligned and uniform as possible.

If you step away from the browser for a second and look at physical things around you, nothing is ever truly uniform.

Take an old letterpress print: the ink bleeds slightly into the paper grain, some letters have a microscopic tilt, and the baseline isn’t always that straight. Or think about a deck of Polaroid photos dropped on a coffee table; those photos aren’t perfect, probably not straight either. Or what about lights flickering in a street at night? That little bit of analog messiness is what makes things feel alive, organic, and human.

On the web, we’ve gotten so good at pixel perfection that sometimes our interfaces end up feeling a bit sterile. We notice this even more now with rapidly created designs by an unguided LLM; we usually end up with the same sort of design we had 10 years ago. Everything is squared off, aligned, neat. It works, but frankly, it does get a bit boring.

Randomness in CSS doesn’t have to mean throwing your design system out the window. It’s about little imperfections and playfulness. Maybe let’s even call it fun.

Recent findings suggest that to see what this actually looks like in practice, I spent a few hours tinkering in CodePen. The demos might feel a bit isolated, but I’m sure that many designers could make the best of this controlled chaos. But before we look at those demos, let’s take a look at the syntax.

Sources indicate that the random() function is specified in CSS Values and Units Module Level 5. It generates a pseudo-random value inside your CSS without needing JavaScript or a build-time Sass loop.

The formal specification looks like this:.

In practice, and across current browser implementations, you can just write comma-separated arguments:.

It won’t be a shocker for most people, but I thought I should at least mention that your minimum and maximum bounds must share the exact same unit type.

It has been revealed that the CSS parser needs to know what dimension it’s dealing with. You can use lengths, angles, time, percentages, or plain unitless numbers:.

If you ever need to combine units, you’ll have to reach for calc() inside the arguments so each side resolves properly.

According to recent reports, the optional third argument is the step size. If you don’t add it, the browser picks from a continuous range. But if you provide a step, it rounds the random value to discrete increments:.

This can be helpful in cases where you want things to jump around a bit, but you still want them to land on your pre-defined grid.

Normally, every time random() is evaluated on a property, it creates an independent random value. But there could be an example where you create a box that sets inline-size and block-size at random, but at the same time you need them to match so the element stays a perfect square.

That’s where the caching key comes in:.

In a recent development, in the latest spec, a bare dashed ident like --square-size shares its seed globally across every element in the document (which would make all cards identical). To keep width and height linked on a single element while giving each card its own independent size, the spec requires pairing it with the element-scoped keyword (e.g. --square-size element-scoped).

It has been revealed that to see this in action, I created a little example. In the top row, the tiles have uncached dimensions, which distorts each tile into an unpredictable, mismatched rectangle. In the bottom row, both inline-size and block-size share --square-size, guaranteeing that each tile remains a pristine 1:1 square. Refresh the CodePen a couple of times and notice the bottom cards keeping the same randomness:.

See the Pen [Uncached vs cached random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e91-4bac-765e-b04e-a53636759163) by @utilitybend.

Because we’re still in the rollout phase, you’ll want to wrap your experiments in @supports:.

Industry observers note that there’s also another function in the spec called random-item(). While random() handles numerical ranges, random-item() lets you pick from a list of predefined tokens or keywords:.

This can be handy to randomise from a set of design tokens. This one does not have any browser support at the moment, but it certainly is something to look forward to.

And now for the practical part.

When I started playing with the feature, I was also doing some typography tricks with animations. So that’s where my first thought went: Typography! What if we just add a tiny bit of imperfection to a word?

According to recent reports, think of vintage book covers. The letters aren’t misaligned by miles, but they have small imperfections.

See the Pen [Imperfection random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-157f-708d-a704-fa067114aaca) by @utilitybend.

Here is the CSS powering the letters:.

Industry observers note that I also added a little hover effect. While you’re reading, the word feels playful. But the second you hover over it, every character snaps back.

According to recent reports, one quick accessibility warning here: If you break a word into separate elements so you can style each letter, screen readers will often read it out as individual characters: “i - m - p - e - r - f - e - c - t - i - o - n”, or pause awkwardly between each one. That’s a terrible user experience.

Always hide the visual spans from assistive tech and provide the full word:.

Screen reader customers get the clean text, and sighted users get the fun visual quirks.

Once I had those letters sitting there with their little tilts, I couldn’t resist: what if we animated it?

According to recent reports, I started tinkering with a bounce keyframe. I was just goofing around, but the end result gave me a little smile. If you animate every letter with the exact same timing, you get that clean sine wave we’ve all seen before. But if every letter gets its own jump height, its own duration, and its own landing squash, suddenly the word looks like a bunch of little characters jumping around on a trampoline.

See the Pen [Bouncy imperfection with CSS random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-c117-729f-9844-ddf19fc1fc96) by @utilitybend.

Here is how the bounce parameters are wired up:.

Notice the negative animation delay (--delay: random(-3s, 0s)).

Sources indicate that if you set a positive delay, the letters sit frozen on page load, waiting for their timers to expire before jumping. By using a negative delay, the browser pretends the animation has already been running for a few seconds. The moment the page loads, every letter is already bouncing at its own rhythm.

We’ve built cards. Lots of cards. So many cards… Portfolio grids, blog summaries, feature lists. And most of the time, they sit in three or four neat, boring columns.

Industry observers note that for dashboards, that’s exactly what you want. But if you’re building a lifestyle portfolio, a children’s website, or a collection of vacation photos, we can be a bit more playful. In the following example, I did just that:.

See the Pen [Random card tilt [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e93-849d-72a9-9254-3f4305e58a34) by @utilitybend.

Here’s how I put that together:.

According to recent reports, in the example, playing around with the shadow was a fun experiment. I will probably try more effects with that in the future.

Recent findings suggest that here is where modern CSS features start getting really interesting. In the previous demo with tilting cards, we used pure randomness. But what if you have a stack of cards that needs to fan out across the screen as you scroll?

In this example, I decided to use math for the structure and randomness for the human imperfection.

See the Pen [Scroll drivin animations with random() tilted cards [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e94-79c6-70b1-97d4-66b7c2d736b0) by @utilitybend.

Look at how cleanly this works:.

If you’ve ever looked at brutalist or high-end fashion websites, you’ve probably seen horizontal marquee text drifting across the screen as you scroll down the page.

Usually, you see developers creating classes like .drift-slow, .drift-fast, .drift-reverse, or using a hefty JavaScript scroll listener to compute transforms.

With random() and a tiny bit of math, we can get procedural drift speeds in just a few lines:.

See the Pen [Random() velocity scroll animation [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-4cbe-77bd-9128-685d2c75cc56) by @utilitybend.

calc(pow(-1, sibling-index())) gives us alternating directions (1, -1, 1, -1), and random(15%, 44%) decides how fast each row travels. As you scroll, each typographic line moves at its own tempo.

Recent findings suggest that I love photography, and one of my favorite things about prime lenses is shallow depth of field. When you shoot at a wide aperture like f/1.7, only whatever is right on your focal plane stays sharp. Everything else melts away into soft bokeh. Yep, photography is all about that bokeh!

By combining random() with filter: blur(), opacity, and scale, we can recreate that lens feel:.

See the Pen [All about that random() bokeh [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-fe50-76dc-943b-d75fcaf704e6) by @utilitybend.

Some words land at blur(0px) with full opacity right in front of your eyes. Others blur out to 6px or 8px and fade into the background. And when you hover over any blurry item in the back, it rack-focuses right into sharpness. It’s a great little effect for decorative hero sections or tag clouds.

Now that we’ve played with the wild side, let’s talk about where this actually belongs in our daily work.

Recent findings suggest that but! I am happy to be proven wrong here. I encourage you to challenge the status quo and experiment with this.

Any time you use animations, you have to respect user preferences for reduced motion:.

If someone prefers reduced motion, it could also be a good idea to flatten the angles, not just the animations. I can imagine that a lot of random angles can also upset people while scrolling. Design should be fun, but never at the cost of accessibility.

Recent findings suggest that tinkering with random() over the last couple of days was a lot of fun. I’m still not sure if I’ll be able to convince my designer friends, but what I do know is that it brings a bit of joy.

Recent findings suggest that whenever we wanted a bit of organic randomness on the web, we had to make compromises: either pull in a JavaScript animation library, or write huge preprocessor loops that spit out hundreds of lines of static CSS. Having this built into the browser engine with zero JavaScript overhead is such a welcome addition.

We spent the last decade mastering consistency, tokens, and design systems. Now that we have that foundation in place, maybe it’s time to let a little bit of playful messiness back onto the web.

I really believe that the web is supposed to be fun.

Never mind the defaults; here is CSS random().

Mutabor Unveils the Voith brand identity

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.
  • Sources indicate that the whole system starts with a single chevron.
  • The custom typeface carries the voice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.

Sources indicate that the whole system starts with a single chevron. Mutabor calls it the V-Vector, a > that points forward and never sits still: it repeats into a pattern on the Appleton reception wall, frames a machine on the launch poster, and turns into punctuation inside the headlines. Voith Blue stays the signature color, and bright tones join it, a vivid royal blue for screens and a mint green for the accent word. On black, "Machines with a digital heart." puts the machine inside the chevron. On blue, "Always breaking fresh ground" lets the green >ground do the talking.

The custom typeface carries the voice. Mutabor drew it only for Voith, and it indicates in the way headlines sit: heavy, round, and set large enough that one line fills a poster. "Hydro driving renewable momentum" runs white on blue with the green >momentum as the punchline, and "Speed press" splits across a dark panel in the same weight. The VOITH wordmark stays in solid capitals, unchanged, while the type around it changes scale.

One frame demonstrates the construction behind it, a lowercase a drawn with node points and thin rules beside a turbine, the letter treated like an engineered part. The grid is visible in the letterform, and the same precision runs through the system, from the wordmark lockup to the small labels on the machine diagrams.

The system proves itself where the manufacturer actually works. The reception wall at Appleton carries the blue V pattern behind "Welcome to Appleton", with the VOITH wordmark set into the desk. Posters, phone screens, documents, and an agenda share the same blue, the same green, and the same chevron, from a "We are hiring" phone card to a "CSH operating principle" diagram. A purple machine close-up is labeled "nanometer precision torque drive", the product photography sitting inside the same graphic language as the posters.

Some of the case imagery is marked AI generated, Mutabor's own label on the frames, and the photography of the plants and machines reads as illustration as much as record. The rollout began in March 2026, after an internal launch in October 2025, and now runs across all markets and touchpoints. It is the first time the three business units, hydropower, papermaking, and drive technology, share one consistent, digitally native identity, and the work took the Red Dot Award for Corporate Design and Identity in 2026.

The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack.
  • Of course, presentation matters, too.
  • Italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack. It invites you to pick it up, lose yourself in its pages, and discover something you didn’t know before. Whether it’s an intimate look at a designer’s creative process, an architectural survey, or a collection of extraordinary photographs, the best examples offer plenty to explore beyond their covers.

Of course, presentation matters, too. Beautiful printing, thoughtful layouts, and striking imagery can turn a book into a design object in its own right. For this year’s selection, we’ve gathered titles that balance visual appeal with compelling content, spanning architecture, interiors, art, photography, and creative culture. They’re books worth giving, displaying, and returning to long after the holidays.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture. Written by design historian Glenn Adamson, this richly illustrated monograph explores Salvagni’s distinctive approach to furniture, lighting, and decorative objects, where classical references meet contemporary forms. Across 336 pages and 246 illustrations, readers get a closer look at his extraordinary use of materials, from bronze and onyx to marble and rare woods.

Achille is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Perched above the Amalfi Coast, Villa Treville was once the private retreat of legendary Italian director Franco Zeffirelli, whose theatrical sensibility shaped the property’s richly layered interiors. Assouline’s Villa Treville Positano takes readers inside the historic estate, exploring its architecture, lush gardens, and eclectic collection of antiques and decorative objects. With more than 200 illustrations and a textured cover inspired by the villa’s patterned ceramic tiles, the book captures the property’s distinctive character inside and out.

Villa Treville Positano is available at shopbop.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

From Charles and Ray Eames to Florence Knoll, the designers who shaped the midcentury movement continue to influence how we live today. Published by Phaidon, this richly illustrated hardcover profiles 300 influential figures, including lesser-known talents whose work deserves a closer look. Spanning furniture, ceramics, glassware, and textiles, it’s an absorbing gift for anyone curious about the history of modern design.

Mid-Century Modern Designers is available at hawkinsnewyork.com for $90.

Photography courtesy of Artisan Books.

From cozy mountain chalets to the rituals that follow a day on the slopes, Après Ski captures the atmosphere of alpine living. Blending interiors, travel, food, and ski culture, the book celebrates a lifestyle that’s as much about gathering around the fire as it is about skiing. A fitting gift for anyone drawn to mountain retreats, whether or not they ever hit the slopes.

Après Ski is available at twowebster.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Porsche enthusiasts will need to clear some serious coffee table space for this oversized tribute to the legendary automaker. Written by A.J. Baime in collaboration with Porsche, the 224-page volume explores 100 defining moments in the brand’s history, from the original 356 to its racing triumphs, design innovations, and collaborations with artists like Daniel Arsham. Archival photography, design sketches, and vintage advertisements reveal Porsche’s influence beyond the automotive world. Handcrafted in Italy, the book comes housed in a padded clamshell featuring a recessed metal image of the iconic Porsche 917K.

Porsche: The Impossible Collection is available at assouline.com for $1,400.

Photography courtesy of Prestel Publishing.

Recent findings suggest that long before botanical photography became commonplace, artist and naturalist Mary Vaux Walcott spent countless hours outdoors capturing the delicate details of North America’s wildflowers in watercolor. Originally published in 1925, her remarkable illustrations are brought together in this oversized volume featuring more than 250 botanical studies. From the subtle variations in petal color to the intricate shapes of leaves and stems, each painting reveals Walcott’s extraordinary eye for detail. Published in association with the Smithsonian Institution, it’s a beautiful intersection of art, science, and nature that deserves a place on the coffee table.

Wild Flowers of North America is available at mcgeeandco.com for $72.

In a recent development, still shopping? Explore Design Milk’s Complete 2026 Holiday Gift Guide for more thoughtful finds for everyone on your list.

Photography courtesy of Maison Plage.

In a recent development, for 100 years, Cahiers d’Art has helped shape the conversation around modern art, championing artists and ideas that challenged convention. Published to celebrate the centennial of the influential Parisian art journal, gallery, and publishing house, A Century of Modernism traces its extraordinary history through archival material, artwork, and contributions from figures including Pablo Picasso, Henri Matisse, and Marcel Duchamp. With approximately 200 illustrations and a striking graphic cover, the book traces the connections between art, design, and publishing.

Cahiers d’Art: A Century of Modernism is available at maisonplage.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Rizzoli.

Sources indicate that for a century, The New Yorker has turned its covers into miniature works of art, capturing everything from everyday New York life to defining cultural moments. Edited by longtime art editor Françoise Mouly, with an introduction by editor-in-chief David Remnick, The New Yorker: From Cover to Cover celebrates that visual legacy through hundreds of illustrations by artists including Saul Steinberg, Roz Chast, Chris Ware, and David Hockney. Spanning 100 years of creativity, the 336-page collection reveals how illustration has shaped the magazine’s distinctive visual identity.

The Upcoming Yorker: From Cover to Cover is available at barnesandnoble.com for $75.

Photography courtesy of Thames & Hudson.

Food, art, and cultural heritage come together in The Art of Korean Cooking, a visually rich exploration of Korea’s culinary traditions. Created by Onjium, a Seoul-based cultural research institute and Michelin-starred restaurant, the book pairs more than 80 recipes with essays exploring the history, ingredients, and techniques behind Korean cuisine. Beautifully composed photography captures everything from seasonal ingredients to finished dishes, revealing the artistry behind each preparation. With 200 illustrations, the 256-page hardcover is as much a celebration of Korean culture and craftsmanship as it is a cookbook.

The Art of Korean Cooking is available at thamesandhudson.com for $47.

Photography courtesy of teNeues.

Not all coffee table books must be about art, architecture, or interiors. Football: The Ultimate Book celebrates America’s favorite sport through striking photography and stories spanning legendary players, iconic stadiums, historic games, and unforgettable Super Bowl moments. This special edition features a handsome black leather-bound cover that gives the 224-page book a sophisticated presence on any coffee table. It’s a winning gift for football fans who appreciate good design.

Football: The Ultimate Book is available at crateandbarrel.com for $200.

Photography courtesy of Taschen.

It has been revealed that from Fred Astaire’s effortless elegance to the exuberance of 1960s dance floors, LIFE. Let’s Dance captures the joy of movement through the lens of Life magazine’s legendary photographers. Published by Taschen, the collection brings together more than 200 archival images, many previously unseen, documenting everything from ballet and ballroom to flamenco and the twist. Spanning the late 1930s through the early 1970s, the photographs are accompanied by original magazine covers and commentary from dance critic Lyndsey Winship, offering a lively look at how dance reflects culture, community, and self-expression.

In a recent development, LIFE. Let’s Dance is available at taschen.com for $50.

Photography courtesy of Wynwood Walls.

Industry observers note that from the streets of Paris to collaborations with Chanel and Louis Vuitton, André Saraiva has built a career around his playful, instantly recognizable graffiti character, Mr. A. Published by Rizzoli, Graffiti Life explores the artist’s creative world through painting, photography, graphic design, fashion, and more. The 320-page hardcover is as expressive as its subject, featuring a vibrant cloth cover with foil lettering and seven pop-ups designed by Saraiva himself. It’s a colorful, interactive celebration of an artist who has never been one to stay within the lines.

André Saraiva: Graffiti Life is available at shop.thewynwoodwalls.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Printworks.

It has been revealed that the most meaningful coffee table book might be the one you fill yourself. Designed to look like a traditional art book, Printworks’ Life Photo Book features a minimalist beige cloth cover with understated white typography. Inside, 40 sheets of high-quality photo paper offer space to preserve favorite memories, from everyday moments to once-in-a-lifetime adventures. Its expandable binding accommodates photographs as they’re added, transforming a beautifully designed object into a personal keepsake.

The Life Photo Book is available at printworksmarket.com for $39.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

Industry observers note that what does contemporary product design look like around the world? Phaidon’s Designed for Life offers a fascinating look at 100 designers pushing the boundaries of furniture, lighting, everyday objects, and more. From established names like Faye Toogood and Sabine Marcelis to emerging talents, the 304-page hardcover explores the materials, techniques, and ideas shaping design today. With 500 illustrations, it’s an inspiring addition to any design enthusiast’s coffee table.

Designed for Life: The World’s Best Product Designers is available at store.hermanmiller.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Taschen.

Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto has spent his career challenging the boundaries between architecture and nature, creating structures that blur the lines between indoors and out. Published by Taschen, Fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today explores three decades of his experimental approach through projects including London’s Serpentine Gallery Pavilion, L’Arbre Blanc in Montpellier, and the Grand Ring at Expo 2025 Osaka. Filled with architectural photography, drawings, and sketches, the oversized, 464-page volume documents the evolution of one of contemporary architecture’s most inventive minds.

Fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today is available for preorder at taschen.com for $200.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

Few people have shaped fashion imagery quite like Grace Coddington. In Grace: The American Vogue Years, the legendary creative director revisits some of her most memorable editorials from 2002 to 2016, including collaborations with photographers Annie Leibovitz, Steven Meisel, and Tim Walker. More than 350 photographs showcase Coddington’s imaginative approach to fashion storytelling, while her behind-the-scenes commentary reveals how the elaborate shoots came together. This updated edition offers a fascinating look at the creative vision behind some of Vogue’s most iconic images.

Grace: The American Vogue Years is available at phaidon.com for $60.

Photography courtesy of Crate & Barrel.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

From maximalist spaces bursting with color to minimalist interiors that celebrate simplicity, Defining Style explores the many ways we make a space our own. Written by Joan Barzilay Freund, the book examines 25 distinct design styles through 150 residential interiors by designers, including spaces by Studio Shamshiri, Laura Gonzalez, and Vincenzo De Cotiis, as well as artist Móyòsóré Martins’ studio. With 260 illustrations and a vibrant, geometric cover, it’s as visually engaging on the coffee table as the spaces featured inside.

Defining Style: The Book of Interior Design is available at phaidon.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Sources indicate that art history gets a playful makeover in Assouline’s Art Game Book, which brings an interactive twist to the traditional coffee table book. Through quizzes, puzzles, games, and essays, author David Rosenberg takes readers from Cubism and Dada to Pop Art and contemporary digital art, featuring icons like Warhol, Basquiat, and Dalí along the way. Newly updated for 2026, the oversized, canvas-bound hardcover makes learning about art feel more like play than homework.

The Art Game Book is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

In a recent development, color takes center stage in Rainbow Dreams, a vibrant exploration of how contemporary artists use the full spectrum to transform their work. Featuring more than 200 artworks by over 100 artists, including Yayoi Kusama, Takashi Murakami, Olafur Eliasson, and Ugo Rondinone, the book spans painting, sculpture, photography, and immersive installations. The 256-page hardcover is a colorful design object in its own right, with a seamless rainbow gradient wrapping around the cover and edges. It’s a joyful addition to any art lover’s collection.

Rainbow Dreams: Color and Light in Contemporary Art is available at phaidon.com for $40.

Art Meets the Slopes at Powder Mountain’s Outdoor Gallery

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most skiers and snowboarders will likely pause at some point during a day on the slopes to take in their surroundings.
  • Recent findings suggest that davina Semo’s Listener (2020–2024), a patinated cast-bronze bell, is part of Powder Art Foundation’s outdoor art collection at Utah’s Powder Mountain.
  • Established in 2024 in partnership with Dia Art Foundation, Powder Art Foundation occupies 8,000 acres of Utah’s Wasatch Mountains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most skiers and snowboarders will likely pause at some point during a day on the slopes to take in their surroundings. After all, ski resorts typically offer great mountain views. But at Powder Mountain in Utah, visitors get more than a scenic view. They might also encounter a bright pink pineapple rising among the pines, a classical Greek column twisted into an improbable shape, or poetry carved into a boulder. These three installations are the latest additions to Powder Art Foundation’s skiable outdoor art museum, an evolving collection that challenges how—and where—we experience art.

Recent findings suggest that davina Semo’s Listener (2020–2024), a patinated cast-bronze bell, is part of Powder Art Foundation’s outdoor art collection at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography courtesy of Powder Art Foundation.

Established in 2024 in partnership with Dia Art Foundation, Powder Art Foundation occupies 8,000 acres of Utah’s Wasatch Mountains. The foundation’s goal is to bring contemporary installations into dialogue with the landscape while honoring the region’s connection to the Land Art movement.

“We’re building a collection that people encounter while spending time outdoors, so I’m interested in work that can surprise you and hold your attention without needing a museum around it,” indicates Alex Zhang, chief creative officer of Powder Mountain.

Schemata Architects Designs a Modern Chalet on Powder Mountain.

In a recent development, this year’s latest installations—from artists Jenny Holzer, Rose Wylie, and Xu Zhen—join an existing collection that includes works by Davina Semo, Nobuo Sekine, Nancy Holt, Kayode Ojo, and others. Each takes a different approach to interacting with the landscape. “I like having that range, rather than one consistent approach to what outdoor sculpture should look like,” Zhang says.

Jenny Holzer’s ‘THE EYE’ (2026), featuring poetry by May Swenson carved into a native quartzite boulder, sits within the forested landscape of Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

According to recent reports, whether skiing in winter or hiking and biking during warmer months, visitors may encounter THE EYE (2026), a new installation by Jenny Holzer. The American neo-conceptual artist conceived of an evolving commission for Powder Mountain centered on work by the late Utah-born poet May Swenson.

Holzer selected a native quartzite boulder already embedded in the mountain, carving a phrase from Swenson’s poetry directly into the stone rather than relocating it or disturbing the surrounding vegetation: “The eye also a sun wanders and all that it sees it owns.”.

A close-up of Jenny Holzer’s ‘THE EYE’ (2026) reveals a line of poetry by May Swenson carved directly into a native quartzite boulder at Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Sources indicate that blending into its natural surroundings, the work could easily go unnoticed by visitors who aren’t looking carefully. As snow, sunlight, and vegetation transform the landscape throughout the year, the inscription offers a point of continuity, even as the experience of encountering it changes.

THE EYE is the first in what Holzer aims to be an ongoing group of carved stones across the mountain. Like this one, future boulders will be selected on the mountain and the art created in place.

Rose Wylie’s ‘Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb’ (2025), a 12-foot-tall painted bronze sculpture inspired by a pineapple she sketched in 2013, stands among towering pine trees at Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Sources indicate that A decidedly different approach comes from Rose Wylie, whose Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb (2025) takes the form of a 12-foot-tall, bright pink painted bronze sculpture. The pineapple-like totem marks Wylie’s first permanent public sculpture in the U.S. The 92-year-old British painter describes the work as “poetic transformation,” which began in 2013 when she purchased a Ghanaian-grown pineapple at a local market. Struck by its distinctive surface and dramatic crown of leaves, she sketched the fruit.

A close-up of Rose Wylie’s ‘Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb’ (2025) highlights the exaggerated crown of leaves that gives the bright pink sculpture its distinctive silhouette. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

It has been revealed that more than a decade later, those drawings have taken on a new dimension. Standing among 50-foot pine trees, the painted bronze sculpture retains the exaggerated silhouette of Wylie’s original sketches. Its form shifts between recognizable fruit, fantastical plant, and something more explosive, suggesting how scale and material can transform an ordinary subject into something entirely unexpected.

According to recent reports, unlike Holzer’s work, which is quite literally part of the scenery, Wylie’s is impossible to miss, its almost cartoonish silhouette creating an unexpected interruption in the natural landscape. Shanghai-based artist Xu Zhen takes yet another approach with Hello (2021–2022), which transforms a classical Corinthian column into a twisting, serpentine form.

Recent findings suggest that xu Zhen’s ‘Hello’ (2021–2022) transforms a classical Corinthian column into a twisting, serpentine sculpture nestled among the aspen trees at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Industry observers note that to develop the sculpture’s serpentine form, Zhen studied the movements of snakes alongside representations of dragons and serpents from different cultures. He ultimately selected the Corinthian column for its ornate capital, whose leaf-like details suggested the head of a living creature. Using a 3D-scanned model as his starting point, he developed the form digitally before producing a full-scale prototype that informed the final bronze casting.

It has been revealed that “My work has always been about discovering alternative forms that an object might take,” the multimedia artist explains. “These forms should feel natural, as though the object was always meant to exist that way, while remaining outside our conventional understanding and experience.”.

According to recent reports, A close-up of Xu Zhen’s Hello (2021–2022) reveals the ornate Corinthian capital, whose leaf-like details give the twisting column an almost creature-like appearance. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Recent findings suggest that installed among the mountain’s aspen trees, Hello takes on what Zhen describes as a “distinctly surreal quality.” Yet the setting also feels surprisingly natural. When he first saw the sculpture at Powder Mountain, the artist recalls feeling “that it had returned to the world where it belongs.”.

For Zhang, the experience of encountering these works is as important as the artworks themselves. “You’re moving, your heart rate is up, there’s adrenaline, and then you come around a corner and encounter a work without expecting it,” he notes. “I think being that engaged in your body changes how you experience the art.”.

Recent findings suggest that visitors to Powder Art Foundation’s fall open house gather around Nobuo Sekine’s Phase of Nothingness – Stone Stack (1970/2025) at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by McCade Gordon for Powder Art Foundation.

Not every work is intended to have the same relationship to the mountain. “Some should feel like you discovered them; others should stop you in your tracks,” Zhang notes. “The mountain connects everything.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Powder Mountain art trail opens for the winter season in mid-December, with lift-accessible installations available from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily and night access to the Sundown area from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. Access to the installations is included with a lift ticket or season pass.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Recent findings suggest that so what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that so what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions? Is there really any noticeable difference between carets, chevrons, arrows, and triangles?

Well, research shows that there is some difference indeed. But what’s more interesting is that split menus are harmful, why it’s better to not have icons and text labels link to different actions, and why the caret is the safest icon choice. Let’s dive in!

The findings aren’t very surprising: without any icon in use, people expect that tapping on the menu item would take them directly to a upcoming page. Users often struggle with custom icons as they don’t clearly signal that they’ll open an accordion. And people tend to tap fairly equally on the icon and on the label for most icons.

In a recent development, many designs (like the one below) tend to slightly overcomplicate things by adding arrows and carets pointing everywhere, depending on the state of the accordion. But typically we don’t need to use an arrow to indicate a link to the category.

Sources indicate that the rule of thumb is very simple: if it’s a link, the easiest and most effective way is to simply underline it — without any arrow, caret, or other icon. Perhaps it’s not particularly exciting, but it works flawlessly every single time.

Using a right-facing arrow icon ▶ isn’t associated with an expectation of going directly to a new page. And having the same icon pointing down ▼ doesn’t necessarily imply that an accordion is going to open on tap/click.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a good idea to avoid split buttons for accordions — where the text label links directly to a page, but the icon opens the accordion. Instead, it’s much more reliable to allow owners to tap on a main category and expose the menu; and to access the category page, we add a link to it inside the menu.

Recent findings suggest that for accordions, we typically use +/− or arrows ↓/↑ to signal expanded and collapsed states, and typically it works well. However, both have many different interpretations. Plus + can mean anything from saving for later to adding to cart to zooming in, and can be particularly confusing for multi-level navigation, with many levels open at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that arrows ↓/↑ can mean scrolling or sliding or finding the next match, but also a jump to a particular portion of a page. Both plus and arrows are well-understood and work, but depending on the design, can be confusing — mostly because they are overloaded.

The safe choice is to use the caret/triangle pointing down ▼ by default, and change it to a caret pointing up or a caret pointing sideways ▶ on interaction. If you need an alternative, then +/- typically work well, too.

Sources indicate that but we certainly don’t need any further icons or arrows to indicate where the links go. The same goes for split menus, which often produce more mistakes than help. Instead, we have one button or dropdown that does exactly one thing — indicates all options and allows consumers to drill down.

Sources indicate that and if you need a direct link, we link the title directly to the page and underline it. More often than not, simpler is better.

  • Chila Kumari Singh Burman in front of her Winter Commission covering the façade of Tate Britain in London in 2020.
  • Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds, which will run until spring 2028, will include work by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray, among others.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tate Liverpool will reopen next autumn following an extensive four-year redevelopment costing around £30m. The relaunch programme includes a major show dedicated to Surrealism along with the first major retrospective for the Liverpool-based artist Chila Kumari Singh Burman. The key regional UK gallery, located on the city’s Royal Albert Dock, closed in October 2023 and was initially due to reopen in 2025.

Chila Kumari Singh Burman in front of her Winter Commission covering the façade of Tate Britain in London in 2020.

Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds, which will run until spring 2028, will include work by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray, among others. “The show will reveal the vital role of Surrealism in the history of theatre and dance, from experiments with masquerade, character and role play to major commissions for stage sets and costumes,” claims a Tate statement. Works featured include Claude Cahun's photograph of Sheila Legge’s 1936 performance Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal, when the artist wore a Dalí-inspired costume in London's Trafalgar Square.

Claude Cahun, Sheila Legge as Surrealist ‘Phantom’, Trafalgar Square (1936).

© Claude Cahun; Image courtesy Jersey Heritage Collections.

In a recent development, for the overhaul, Tate Liverpool received £18.6m from the Public Bodies Infrastructure Fund, which is awarded by the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. It also received philanthropic donations from the Garfield Weston Foundation (£3m), the Wolfson Foundation (£1.25m) and the Ross Warburton Charitable Trust, alongside other trusts and individuals.

The UK Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government also awarded £10m to the gallery, which it secured through a combined £20m bid with National Museums Liverpool. “We have raised more [than £30m] because there are other costs associated with reinstalling and reopening the museum,” a Tate spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper.

According to a Tate statement, the designs for the upcoming gallery, drawn up by 6a architects, “open up spaces to display the incredible variety of Tate’s collection and host world-class exhibitions. These galleries will sit alongside new public spaces for play, relaxation and learning with views across the Mersey, helping to connect the gallery with the city and the communities that surround it.” The New York and Berlin-based artist Asad Raza will create the first major commission for the gallery’s Art Hall.

It has been revealed that tate Liverpool, which opened in 1988, was designed by James Stirling who converted the northwest corner of a seven-story warehouse standing on the Royal Albert Dock into the five-storey gallery. It received 405,000 visitors in 2022, its last full year, and 660,000 in 2019, before the Covid-19 pandemic.

It has been revealed that helen Legg stepped down as Tate Liverpool director earlier this year, with Jemima Pyne taking over in the interim; a fresh director will be recruited after the new director of Tate, Jessica Morgan, is in post next year, the spokesperson confirmed. Tate comprises four galleries: Tate Modern, Tate Britain, Tate Liverpool and Tate St Ives.

  • Sources indicate that milkshake is a Stockholm label, a division of Sony Music Entertainment founded in 2019, and its latest identity starts in a car.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

STUDIO HERRSTRÃM rebuilds the Milkshake brand identity around car culture, a redrawn splash mark, high-vis color and road signs.

Sources indicate that milkshake is a Stockholm label, a division of Sony Music Entertainment founded in 2019, and its latest identity starts in a car. The name was suggested on a car ride, milestones happened in cars, and new music was taken for a car test. The old splash is still there, redrawn as a rounded, blended symbol that reads like metal and liquid merging, and the wordmark runs through it with a zigzag cut that splits Milkshake into two stacked hits. On the posters the name fills the frame until the letters stop being text and start being the picture: acid yellow Milksh across the top, shake across the bottom.

It has been revealed that the type system is Gates, a neo-grotesque from Contextype, shown in the specimen with arrows, asterisks, circled letters and roman numerals on a mauve field. The wordmark itself leans forward, its letters cut on a slant that matches the splash, and the supporting lockups borrow their logic from car window stickers and milk carton nutrition labels: small blocks of capitals that hold track names, release dates and the p-line symbol without breaking the grid.

The system proves itself on the objects it touches. A high-vis vest carries the full lockup on its back in black on acid yellow, with reflective bands borrowed from road markings. A neon green acrylic cube hangs outside the shopfront with the black wordmark on its face. A blender wears the whole icon set as stickers: the machine that makes the drink becomes the merch.

Sources indicate that color does the rest. Acid yellow is the signal color, while neon pink and soft lilac take the flavor cues and black keeps the contrast high. The same palette runs the subway poster for Tove Lo's single Me/You (always and forever), dated 18.09.26. Linn Wexell, founder and creative director of Milkshake, claims the creative work was smart and on point and the visuals stunning.

Fireclay Tile Turns Traditional Textiles Into Hand-Painted Tile

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Plaids and florals might seem more at home on upholstery or wallpaper than ceramic tile, but Fireclay Tile’s latest collection makes a compelling case for bringing those familiar patterns to harder surfaces.
  • Interestingly, the collection didn’t begin with flowers at all.
  • Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection in its Winter palette, featuring deep blues, earthy greens, and warm neutrals across floral, striped, and plaid patterns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plaids and florals might seem more at home on upholstery or wallpaper than ceramic tile, but Fireclay Tile’s latest collection makes a compelling case for bringing those familiar patterns to harder surfaces. Called Idyllwild, the new hand-painted collection takes inspiration from traditional textiles, translating everything from delicate botanical illustrations to richly layered plaids into ceramic designs that feel both nostalgic and contemporary.

Interestingly, the collection didn’t begin with flowers at all. “We were seeing designers use a lot of intricate textiles, colors, and patterns together,” explains Jamie Chappell, VP of Brand and Product at Fireclay Tile, adding that early explorations focused on plaids and stripes. “As a true lover of ’90s alt-rock, I actually went down a rabbit hole early on, wondering if it should be a ‘grunge’ collection.”.

Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection in its Winter palette, featuring deep blues, earthy greens, and warm neutrals across floral, striped, and plaid patterns.

That direction eventually gave way to something softer. Recognizing the longstanding relationship between florals and plaids in interiors, the team introduced botanical patterns to balance the collection’s more structured designs. The name Idyllwild followed, referencing the California mountain town.

The resulting collection includes 16 patterns organized into four categories: Specimen Flowers, Idyllwild Florals, Idyllwild Stripes, and Idyllwild Plaids.

The Specimen Flowers series features four individual botanical motifs—Allium, Carnation, Lily, and Bluebell—hand-painted on ceramic tile. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

Specimen Flowers features four individual botanical designs—Allium, Carnation, Lily, and Bluebell—that can be arranged across backsplashes, niches, and accent walls. The Idyllwild Florals take a more expansive approach, with repeating patterns named Pomegranate, Tulip, Morning Glory, and Meadow. Their overlapping stems, leaves, and blossoms create the dense, layered effect of a garden growing beyond its boundaries.

According to recent reports, the Stripes and Plaids explore a different kind of ornamentation. Four striped patterns—Stuga, Mokki, Blockhaus, and Thatch—introduce rhythm through repeated lines and geometric details. The Plaids, meanwhile, borrow the visual language of woven fabrics, with Chalet, Highlands, Minka, and Torp creating intersecting grids that can read as anything from understated texture to a bold, room-enveloping pattern.

In a recent development, the Idyllwild Plaids series features four geometric patterns inspired by traditional woven textiles, shown here in warm shades of burgundy, pink, and brown. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

In a recent development, while the designs reference traditional textiles, translating them into hand-painted ceramic required a different way of thinking about pattern. “We had to simplify and edit the artwork so our painting team could actually execute it by hand,” Jamie states.

The process uses resist lines to define individual areas of color, making the scale and spacing of each detail particularly notable. “When we translate intricate woven textiles into screen art, we have to pay very close attention to the thickness of the lines, how small the fields are to fill in, and making sure the painters have enough natural ‘starts and stops’ so they can work efficiently,” Jamie says.

A closer look at Fireclay Tile’s hand-painting process, with glaze applied to the Allium motif from the Idyllwild Specimen Flowers series. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

Fireclay’s painting team was closely involved in prototyping, providing feedback on details that were too small or areas where the glaze couldn’t be applied smoothly. The company also developed a new glaze base specifically for the hand-application process.

Industry observers note that the relationship between design and production extends to color. Each of the 16 patterns is available in four curated palettes inspired by the seasons, but developing those options required another significant undertaking.

The Meadow pattern from Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild Florals series features an assortment of botanical motifs in the Spring color palette. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

Industry observers note that fireclay’s previous hand-painted palette had become disconnected from its broader ceramic offering, limiting customization opportunities. To address that, the production team spent months matching the firm’s 50 core ceramic colors in both gloss and matte finishes. The resulting 100 finishes can be combined across the collection.

A selection of floral, plaid, and striped patterns from Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection, shown in the Winter palette of deep blues, muted greens, and warm neutrals. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

Sources indicate that to develop Idyllwild’s seasonal palettes, the team worked with physical tile samples alongside 4K renderings, testing combinations before translating them into paint sheets for production. The color stories also reflect shifts the company has been observing in interiors, including an interest in deeper reds and earthy blues.

2027 Colors of the Year: The Shades Defining Design.

“Organizing the collection into four seasonal motifs really demonstrates how much color shifts the personality of a design: a plaid in soft pastels feels light and cottage-like, whereas that same pattern in deep, moody tones reads like a cozy wool blanket,” Jamie explains.

Sources indicate that the Idyllwild Stripes series features four hand-painted patterns—Stuga, Mokki, Blockhaus, and Thatch—combining linear details and geometric motifs in shades of blue, green, and brown. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

The collection also introduces latest sizes, including 2-by-8-inch and 3-by-6-inch tiles, designed to work alongside standard field tiles. This allows patterns to be introduced selectively or carried across larger surfaces, with stripes used as borders or accents and more intricate designs covering entire walls.

Although Idyllwild draws from traditional patterns, the finished designs are shaped as much by the practical demands of hand-painting as by their textile references.

Davis Furniture and jehs+laub Introduce the Sculptural Laken Nesting Tables

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Designed to nest seamlessly or stand alone, the three round tables scale from a single grouping to individual pieces.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, three steel parts shape the silhouette of the Laken Occasional Table Series: a spun cone settling low against the floor, a slender column drawing upward from its center, and a second cone opening wide to cradle a circular top. The dual-cone composition gives jehs+laub’s design for Davis Furniture its distinctly modern profile, extended to a set of three nesting tables.

Designed to nest seamlessly or stand alone, the three round tables scale from a single grouping to individual pieces. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Laken continues a collaboration between Davis and jehs+laub that began in 2009, and it carries forward the studio’s approach to balancing soft curvature with precise, architectural form. On every Laken table, gentle radii and careful proportions ease the move from flared base to slender column to inverted cone, and each piece appears fully resolved from any angle.

Nested together or used on their own, the tables can be layered into a single, dynamic arrangement or spread throughout an interior, adapting to lounge, hospitality, and collaborative environments.

Industry observers note that each round tabletop is supported by an inverted steel cone. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

The sculptural form belies a carefully engineered base. Its spun steel cones and steel column are mechanically fastened through concealed hardware for a tight, durable assembly built to perform over time, and a ballast hidden within the lower cone brings the center of gravity down, giving the tables stability and resistance to tipping.

Available in three sizes, Laken Tables offer a wide range of tabletop materials and over 35 powder coat finishes for the steel bases. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

In a recent development, rob Easton, Vice President of Design + Development at Davis, traces the work back to the project’s earliest goals: “The development of Laken was driven by a desire to create a table that feels both visually light and structurally grounded. By breaking the base into a three-part assembly, we were able to refine the proportions, improve serviceability, and integrate stability directly into the form. Every decision was intentional, balancing engineering with the purity of the design.”.

Laken adapts to a range of lounge, hospitality, and collaborative environments, whether the tables are used together or apart. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Industry observers note that tabletops are offered in wood veneer, FENIX® Innovative Materials, and standard laminate. Veneer choices include ash, oak, and walnut, while laminates span solid colors and curated wood grains. The steel base can be finished in any of Davis’ 35-plus powder coats to coordinate with the firm’s broader material palette, and standard felt glides help protect floors.

Tabletops come in wood veneer, FENIX® Innovative Materials, and laminate, with bases in more than 35 powder coat finishes. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

In a recent development, designers Markus Jehs and Jürgen Laub approached the series as a study in composition. “Laken is about clarity of form and the relationship between elements,” they explain. “We were interested in creating a silhouette that feels continuous, where each component contributes to a unified expression.” Between the weighted base and the widening top, the design holds a subtle tension that reads as both soft and exacting.

Distinctive and adaptable, Laken reflects Davis’ commitment to design-driven furniture that brings together performance, materiality, and enduring form.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leonardo Pertileâs book design for ADI Design Museumâs Compasso dâOro packs 1,040 pages into twin cloth volumes set in OT Marmo.

According to recent reports, compressing nearly seventy years of Italian industrial design into a 1,040-page brick isnât a subtle problem. Presented by Fondazione ADI, ADI Associazione per il Disegno Industriale, and ADI Design Museum, this Treccani monograph is edited by Beppe Finessi and designed by Leonardo Pertile as twin cloth editions. Brick-red cloth printed in royal blue marks the English Historical Collection with a yellow ribbon, while yellow cloth inked in red identifies the Italian Collezione Storica with a navy ribbon. Neither cover uses product photography. A large blind-debossed compass presses into the woven board under Omnitypeâs pre-release OT Marmo capitals, and opening the red cover flashes yellow endpaper beside three tall floor lamps.

Industry observers note that according to the museumâs notes, the publication holds 2,275 images across three parts: ADI Design Museumâs archival role, the 1954â2022 Compasso dâOro Roll of Honour, and critical essays and interviews. Pertile keeps that scale legible by shifting the grid per section so the book design doesnât lose its rhythm. On pages 154 and 155, Anty Panseraâs essay wraps justified columns around four staggered black-and-white ceremony photos. Another spread runs a hand-drawn nebido logo study on millimeter graph paper across the top above justified prose and hanging-indent captions citing Franco Albini, Franca Helg, and Bob Noorda. Turn to pages 474 and 475 for Anno 1967 and the density jumps â Enzo Mariâs concentric Freud Opere sketches and Mario Piazzaâs ruled pull quote face Olivettiâs tight vertical matrix of color-coded marks.

Heavy catalogs donât work without quiet spreads. Page 577 pairs an overhead photo of a terracotta sofa and dark-green chaise directly above twin framed floor plans, leaving the plate clear of clutter. That open air widens in the essays and interviews. Alberto Saibeneâs Milano, 1954: cultura e industria opener floats OT Marmo headings high in white space above two narrow columns. On page 967, Beppe Finessiâs interview with Paola Antonelli switches to ragged-right text with outdented BF and PA initials in the margin so speakers scan fast. Itâs disciplined book design that makes a 1,040-page institutional archive easy to open and read.

Dr.Me and Waiting Room Press turn torn street posters into a 400-page book design, hand-ripping every cover of Accidental Collage.

According to recent reports, every copy of Accidental Collage arrives damaged on purpose. Created by Manchester studio Dr.Me and published by Waiting Room Press, the 400-page volume documents weathered billboard strata pulled from city walls. According to Itâs Nice That, Dr.Meâs Mark âEddyâ Edwards drew the cover idea from book artist Lydia Davies, who purposefully defiled the edges of her poetry books. That choice hits before the spine even opens. On the cover, bold sans-serif capitals stack vertically down the right edge, sliced diagonally by a physical paper tear: black letters sit on creased white stock above the rip, flipping to white ink over raw ochre pasteboard and red scraps underneath. It doesnât observe street decay from a polite distance. The book behaves like a city hoarding itself.

Inside, the book design drops white margins completely. Full-bleed photographs push straight to the trim edges, anchored only by tiny centered folios along the bottom border so nothing interrupts the torn paper layers. Thereâs no border competing for attention, so cross-gutter pairings drive the pace. On pages 74 and 75, two ripped portraits lock eyes across the fold â a face peeking through jagged olive-green stenciled stock opposite a monochrome eye buried under white shreds and a red slash. Turn to page 259 and red lips above torn yellow ribbons face giant blue halftone teeth bordered by an exposed CMYK color bar. Elsewhere, pages 312 and 313 pair a shredded magenta portrait and clipped white serif type against a violet sheet torn across the middle to reveal a mouth and ghosted lettering.

It has been revealed that edwards told Itâs Nice That the archive grew after lockdowns as a community began trading found dÃ©collages from Manhattan building hoardings, Parisian metro walls, and London Underground theatre posters. Interviews and essays by Sarah Boris, Nick Deakin, Braulio Amado, and experimental drummers Hisham Akira Bharoocha and Jeremy Gustin sit alongside the plates, linking ripped street bills to rhythm and print culture. On pages 354 and 355, a shredded gig poster dated 09.11.24 faces bold white ON A MISSION FOREVER lettering ripping open over yellow underlayers. Thatâs the discipline behind this book design: strip away gallery framing and let ruined commercial print hold the page on its own.

Latest Update: The Volvo EX60 Draws on Forest Walks and Nordic Seas

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, “Scandinavian design never shouts, but when you come closer, you are rewarded,” claims Sara Erichsen Susnjar, senior color and material design manager at Volvo Cars.
  • Sources indicate that erichsen Susnjar, who has spent 20 years at Volvo Cars, oversaw color and materials for both the EX60 and the EX60 Cross Country.
  • It has been revealed that gathering began close to home, on outings that were already part of the team’s routine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “Scandinavian design never shouts, but when you come closer, you are rewarded,” claims Sara Erichsen Susnjar, senior color and material design manager at Volvo Cars. Detail by detail, the automaker’s new all-electric EX60 bears this out. Its seats carry a pattern drawn from two seas converging off the coast of Skagen, Denmark; its base carpet borrows its hue from foraged finds from the woods outside the company’s studio in Sweden; and an interior lighting option fills the cabin with the silhouettes of leaves.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

Sources indicate that erichsen Susnjar, who has spent 20 years at Volvo Cars, oversaw color and materials for both the EX60 and the EX60 Cross Country. Under her direction, the team looked to the natural world for the car’s colors, patterns, and textures, often starting with what turned up on a walk.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

It has been revealed that gathering began close to home, on outings that were already part of the team’s routine. “We are very fortunate to have the forest just outside our design studio, so it naturally becomes part of our everyday life, whether we go there for lunch, a coffee break, or simply to clear our minds,” Erichsen Susnjar claims.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

Over time, the team began bringing small pieces of the landscape back inside: mushrooms, twigs, stones, moss, and herbs. Each was studied for its pattern, color, and texture, then cast or digitized, and the findings became prompts for fresh ideas. Traces of the work appear in subtle patterns on the seatbacks and door panels, as well as in the shade of the base carpet. As Erichsen Susnjar puts it, “In that sense, a little piece of the forest has found its way into the car.”.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

According to recent reports, inside the cabin, material options include tailored wool-blend upholstery and ash wood decor, which sit alongside a 15-inch curved OLED display with Google built-in. “I think bringing natural materials into such a technical and precise environment creates a beautiful contrast,” Erichsen Susnjar explains. “They bring warmth, character and, in a way, a soul to the car. Because natural materials have their own variations and imperfections, they can never be exactly replicated, which means every interior becomes slightly unique.”.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

Erichsen Susnjar places the cabin’s finer details, including its piping, within a longer regional tradition. “Scandinavian design is very much about those subtle touches,” she claims. “They don’t demand your attention, but you discover them over time.”.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

The EX60 offers six lighting colors, along with Forest Leaves Projection, which brings a canopy of foliage into the interior. The idea came from one of the specialist designers at Volvo Cars, and the team expanded on it to explore how the cabin might feel immersed in woodland.

Outside the cabin, the EX60’s exterior paint colors, among them Forest Lake and Heather Bronze, were developed as a palette that balances light and dark, warm and cool, and complements the colors chosen for the interior. Heather Bronze takes its cue from metals weathered over time and the warm cast of heather fields in autumn.

The EX60’s signature motif began when members of the team visited Skagen, where the Skagerrak and Kattegat seas meet, and observed the patterns created by their intersecting waves. Early sketches were refined into a pattern that now appears across the car. It is perforated into the ventilated Nordico upholstery and applied to the subwoofer mesh, the decor panels of the Core version, the rubber floor mats, and the knitted, ventilated seats of the EX60 Cross Country.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

Beyond its connection to the Danish coastline, the crossing-wave form also proved useful in production. “There is another layer in this story, and that’s how a pattern like crossing waves was perfect for optimizing the cutting of the materials and minimizing waste,” Erichsen Susnjar says. “And because of that, none of the seats look the same.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Giga rebuilds AD Italia for its 45th anniversary: the AD Italia redesign pairs Arizona type, Ghirri colour and a modernist grid.
  • Industry observers note that the first thing you see is the masthead.
  • According to recent reports, proportion went to the type.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giga rebuilds AD Italia for its 45th anniversary: the AD Italia redesign pairs Arizona type, Ghirri colour and a modernist grid.

Industry observers note that the first thing you see is the masthead. AD sits in black flared serif on a soft pink field, the letters drawn wide enough to carry the cover on their own, and the same confidence runs through the glitch. Inside, the November pages open on a white field with SPAZI set large in the same face, issue N.530, and the spreads that follow give each photograph a full page of air. The palette stays soft and everyday: coral, pale green and pale blue, the colours of an Italian landscape rather than a brand manual.

According to recent reports, proportion went to the type. Arizona, by Dinamo Typefaces, is almost a sans with flared strokes, and it brings the measure of Roman inscriptions to the page. A specimen page sets names in Arizona Flare Light, one per line, with nothing else on the field, and the same face carries the cover lines: SPAZI across a white cover, LA NOSTRA GUIDA AL SALONE 2025 stacked in white on black. The letters do the talking, and the layout stays out of their way.

In a recent development, essentiality went to the grid. Giga built it on the logic of modern art catalogues: photographs get room of their own, captions stay small and precise, and the editorial pages stand apart from the advertising around them. A spread on David Bowie runs green panels beside a column of text that starts in 1972, when Bowie became Ziggy Stardust, and a grid of anniversary spreads collects 45 icons from the magazine's history on a single page.

Colour went to Luigi Ghirri. The case page sets the palette beside three everyday Italian landscapes, a canal road, green houses against the sea, a beach with swings, all in the soft register of Ghirri's photographs. The system names its colours plainly: PMS 2344 C coral, PMS 2260 C pale green, PMS 290 C pale blue, each with its hex code printed beside it, the way a printer would want it.

Wit went to the rhythm. Like Ettore Sottsass's Carlton bookcase, which slants its shelves and still holds books, the system plays with its own conventions, varying titles and images from story to story. The redesign debuted with the November 2026 glitch and a room at PAC Milano built around one line: perfect proportions, essential function, a joke, the colours of every day.
