Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex

📅 2026-11-03 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gabriel is a front-end developer and technical writer.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gabriel is a front-end developer and technical writer. He specializes in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Vue, TailwindCSS, and BootStrap, with a track record of … More about Gabriel ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor? You replace ResizeObserver with a container query, the diff is mostly red, and everyone approves it before lunch.

This was what it looked like before you made the change:.

See the Pen [demo (before PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVJq) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

Then, a week later, a card on the dashboard has vanished. A heading has grown on tablets for no reason anyone can explain. The spacing inside a comment is off.

See the Pen [demo (after PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/gbmBopp) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

In a recent development, none of these bugs are in the few lines you wrote. All of them arrived with those few lines of CSS.

In my last article on how CSS is growing smarter, I left a few questions hanging at the end, including: What happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, and how do we debug conditional styles without a clear view of what triggered them? This article is my attempt to answer these two questions.

In a recent development, I think it’s worth saying clearly that I am not saying modern CSS is bad. What I am saying is that:.

A CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about if you don’t understand how it relates to existing code, be it CSS or JavaScript.

Think of a latest CSS feature as a new tenant moving into a shared apartment. The tenant may be quiet and tidy, but they still share a kitchen with everyone who already lives there. In that case, CSS is now roommates with JavaScript, the component’s layout, the CSS Cascade, and the browser’s rendering engine. The apartment’s stability depends less on the tenant and more on how they get along with one another.

That gives us two different things to measure, and a diff only shows the first one:.

I am not the only one thinking about this. In April 2026, Igor Roztropiński published an essay titled “Modern Frontend Complexity: essential or accidental?” asking:.

Recent findings suggest that the essay landed on r/programming, where the thread has drawn 80-plus comments and the replies pull in two directions. One of the most upvoted comments, from a user named Kwantuum, pushes back on the whole genre:.

Another commenter, kayinfire, takes the other side, arguing that “there are tons of scenarios where a front-end framework introduces more accidental complexity than it’s worth.” They say this a few replies later:.

Recent findings suggest that I think both commenters are on to something, and this article lives in the gap between the two. Yes, CSS has improved in the last several years. And yes, “less” CSS on paper is not automatically “less” complexity in practice. That mentioned, my claim is narrower. A native feature only reduces complexity when it actually replaces what was there before and doesn’t disrupt the calm state of everything else it interacts with.

Let’s meet the housemates in our metaphorical apartment, one scenario at a time.

Recent findings suggest that the first housemate is JavaScript, and the trouble starts when the old tenant never quite moves out. Here is a card that switches to a two-column layout when it has enough room. The original version uses a ResizeObserver to toggle a class:.

With CSS Container Queries, we need no script at all and can simplify our selectors at the same time:.

In a recent development, lovely. Now, here’s the thing: migrations rarely happen in one clean sweep. The pull request adds the @container rule and removes the .card--wide .card__body rule. The observer survives because it is registered in another file. The .card--wide .card__title rule survives because nobody searched for the class. Nothing looks broken, because both implementations agree on 480px. Then a designer asks to move the breakpoint to 600px, and a developer updates the only place they know about: the @container rule.

See the Pen [Scenario 1: The Behaviour With Two Owners [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/ZYeqvpx) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

According to recent reports, between 480px and 600px, the card now has a single-column body and a wide-layout title. Nobody wrote that state. To find it, you need to know that the layout has two owners and read both of them.

The same trap comes in other shapes:.

It has been revealed that CSS and JavaScript can happily share a component. What they cannot share is the component’s behavior. So, instead of having a silent fight over a component’s behavior, check first. Know all the contending parties, then split the work.

According to recent reports, and when you’re done migrating, you have to finish the job: delete the observer, the class, and every selector that mentions the class. Otherwise, you may wind up with a tenant who simply refuses to move out.

Back in 2023, I wrote about how block formatting contexts solve float concerns. Back then, creating a block formatting context was something we did on purpose. Today, you can create one without meaning to. When we declare container-type: inline-size, we think we are saying, “let my children query my width.” The browser hears quite a bit more. This is the second housemate, the layout around the component, and our new tenant who just asked for one shelf has ended up rearranging the living room.

It has been revealed that according to MDN’s container-type reference, the value “applies style and inline-size containment to the element.” And MDN’s guide to block formatting contexts lists “query containers (elements where container-type isn’t normal)” among the CSS styles that create one. An element that establishes a upcoming block formatting context will, in MDN’s words:.

That means one declaration can change three layout behaviors that have nothing to do with queries, plus a fourth that comes from inline-size containment. I built a demo where each “before” and “after” pair differs by only that one declaration.

See the Pen [Scenario 2: The Card That Vanished [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/dPvgJpB) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

A paragraph with margin-bottom: 16px sits above the card, and the card’s heading has margin-top: 24px. Before the change, the heading’s margin collapsed through the top of the card and merged with the paragraph’s margin, leaving a 24px gap. Afterward, the margin remained trapped inside the card. The two margins now add up to 40px, and the card grows from 30px to 54px tall.

Sources indicate that the card follows a floated image. Before the change, the card’s box ran behind the float and its text wrapped around the image. Afterward, the whole card sits beside the float; it starts 120px further in (the width of the image) and is 120px narrower.

This is the one that makes cards vanish. Inline-size containment stops an element from taking its width from its contents. MDN has a nice, succinct explanation:.

It has been revealed that in the last demo, three tag-sized cards sit in a flex row and measure roughly 74px, 96px, and 114px, respectively. If we add container-type: inline-size, then all three measure 0px. I got the same 0px result when the card was displayed inline-block, floated, set to a width: fit-content box, was an align-items: flex-start child of a column flex container, and when it was an item in an auto grid track. A plain block-level card retains its full width because its width is determined by its parent rather than its contents.

In a recent development, in isolation, the card is a block that fills its parent. In reality, it is a flex item, follows a float, or sits under a paragraph whose margin it used to absorb.

Before you add container-type to an element, ask yourself the following three questions:.

Answering these will help prevent a housemate from completely changing the furniture layout right from under you.

The third housemate is the CSS Cascade. Every shared apartment has house rules about who gets the last word, and a latest tenant can arrive with more say than anyone expected.

In a recent development, the :has() selector and native nesting let us write short selectors in CSS. But short selectors can match more and weigh more than they appear.

It has been revealed that say we want to remove paragraph margins from card components that have a hero image. This might look like it does the job:.

See the Pen [Scenario 3: The Selector That Reached Too Far [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/pvexpRd) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

This card has no hero image. Yet every paragraph in it loses its margin.

If you inspect the comment’s paragraph in DevTools and look at the “Styles” pane, you will find two culprits:.

It could get even more complex and difficult to catch because the state changes at runtime. Let’s say a user posts a comment that includes an avatar. The body text of the card above it loses its spacing. Good luck reproducing that from a bug report that says “spacing looks off sometimes.”.

The fix is to constrain the selector with child combinators:.

This helps the selector get more specific about what it is yelling about.

Native nesting has the same habit. MDN’s guide to nesting and specificity says the & selector takes “the largest specificity in the associated selector list,” exactly like :is(). Look at this adaptation of MDN’s example:.

A .button link inside a .card is blue, even though the #featured ID is nowhere near it. The usual reaction is a more specific .button rule, then an exception to that rule. Before you know it, you are in a war of specificity you never knew you had declared.

The way out is to keep the selector list and drop its weight by wrapping it in :where():.

In a recent development, plain links inside a card are still blue, and the .button link is red again. Again, another way to quiet the loud housemate.

In a recent development, don’t be fooled into thinking specificity is the whole story. MDN’s introduction to the cascade puts origin, importance, and cascade layers ahead of specificity, and notes that “normal layered styles have less precedence than normal unlayered styles.” In my test, a layered rule with a specificity of 0-4-0 lost to an unlayered .title (0-1-0). So if your new component styles go into @layer components while the legacy stylesheet stays unlayered, the legacy rule wins every conflict, however carefully you wrote the new one. The exception is when the !notable keyword is used, because it actually reverses the cascade order.

Recent findings suggest that miriam Suzanne’s original proposal for cascade layers describes exactly the pain layers were meant to remove: having to “be very careful with matching specificity to layer.” Layers do remove it, but only when the rules on both sides of the conflict are layered. A half-layered codebase just gives you one more ordering to keep in your head.

None of these battles started with :has() or nesting. In an r/webdev thread titled “CSS-in-JS: What’s the biggest performance drop you actually felt?”, one of the most upvoted answers isn’t about performance at all. It is about the cascade:.

This is about the “order of appearance,” which is the last step in the cascade that ends up deciding a conflict nobody knew existed. Another commenter in the subreddit adds that the injected styles can land in a different order in development and production builds: “Who doesn’t love debugging something that works locally but not in prod.”.

According to recent reports, not everyone in the thread agrees on who is to blame. TheThirdRace replies, “It’s a coding glitch, not a technology issue.”.

I think both are right, and that is exactly the point. CSS-in-JS is a different technology from the native features we are looking at, so take this as a neighboring example, not as proof. But the shape of the problem is the same: the tool did what it promised, and the trouble arose from how it complied with the existing rules.

“We moved it to CSS, so it’s faster now.” You have probably heard this in a code review, and maybe mentioned it yourself. In my last article, I warned that it isn’t always the case. Let’s test it.

Industry observers note that moving a behavior from JavaScript to CSS changes who does the work. It doesn’t tell you how much work there is. The last housemate, the browser’s rendering engine, is the one who gets the bill. Everyone in the apartment shares it, and nobody looks at it after the move.

According to recent reports, take :has() as an example. Browser vendors were worried about its cost from the start. In a CSS Working Group issue about :has() restrictions, Emilio Cobos Álvarez noted that implementations wanted to ship it with limitations “in order to prevent performance footguns and complexity.” Today, MDN’s :has() page has a whole section on performance with two pieces of advice:.

I wanted numbers, so I built a list with 5,000 rows. The test toggles an .is-selected class on the same row 300 times, so the row’s selected state changes on every toggle, and forces a style and layout patch each time. I ran it in Chrome 153 on a Mac in October 2026, and recorded a trace in DevTools to count how many elements each toggle restyles.

See the Pen [Scenario 4: The Rewrite Nobody Measured [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVgP) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

There are two lessons in that table.

In a recent development, first, the “bad” selector was fine. Rule 2 is exactly the shape MDN warns against: a :has() anchored to body. It cost about a millisecond and a half more than the script, and it restyled a single element, the toolbar. A frame at 60Hz lasts 16.7ms, so I would take that trade for deleting an event handler any day.

Second, two harmless rules were not harmless together. Rule 3 styles the rows, and its :has() condition remains unchanged throughout the test. On its own, it costs nothing measurable. Put it in the same stylesheet as the second rule instead, and every toggle restyles all 5,000 rows plus the toolbar. That is about what it costs a script to restyle every row on purpose.

Industry observers note that let’s keep this in proportion. Since 7ms still fits inside a frame, nobody would notice it on this page. However, the browser is now restyling 5,001 elements to change just one, and neither rule indicates so. Also, the cost grows with the list. When I set the demo to 20,000 rows, the two rules together restyled 20,001 elements and took about 31ms per toggle, which is nearly two frames.

It has been revealed that I can tell you what Chrome does here, but not why. Changing .is-selected on one row restyles every element that the other :has() rule targets, even though that rule never mentions .is-selected and its result never changes. I have filed this with the Chromium team as an concern, with a reduced test case, and I only tested Chrome. Whatever the cause, neither rule looks suspicious in a code review, and the cost applies only when both are met.

Recent findings suggest that that is system complexity in a single table. And please take the pattern from it, not the numbers: this is one page, one browser, and one machine.

It has been revealed that the same goes for animation. The animation guide on web.dev recommends restricting animations to opacity and transform where possible, and warns that “an animation that moves an element using something other than transform is likely to be slow.” MDN’s CSS performance guide lists the properties that trigger layout when animated, such as width, height, margin, top, and left. A CSS transition on left runs layout on every frame, while a JavaScript animation of transform skips it. The property determines the cost, regardless of which language you write it in.

To be fair, CSS often wins. A script that reads layout, writes styles, and reads layout again forces the browser to do layout several times in one frame, and a container query hands that whole job to the browser. But that win is something you can measure, so measure it:.

Each of these scenarios is small on its own. The trouble is that a real migration could hit all four scenarios at once. You have already seen three of them. They are the three bugs in the “after” demo at the top of this article. Add a long list, and you get the fourth. One move-in, four housemates disturbed.

Sources indicate that A team replaces a card’s JavaScript-driven responsive layout with a container query and :has(). The pull request adds twelve lines of CSS, deletes one script, and misses another. Within a month, three bug reports land, and there’s a chance a performance trace turns up as the fourth problem:.

Industry observers note that none of these reports means that container queries or :has() were the wrong choice. Each bug lives in the meeting point between the fresh CSS and the system it moved into. Still, one small pull request has sent a developer through the JavaScript, the page layout, the cascade, and the profiler.

And the way out is not a return to JavaScript. Here is the same page once more, fixed.

See the Pen [demo (fixed PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/wBJYpPJ) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

It still uses a container query and :has(), with three changes:.

This gap between a clean start and a real codebase shows up in the same r/webdev thread. The person who started it, JRM_Insights, opens with an observation that could describe any of our four scenarios:.

Further down, mq2thez describes moving an old CSS-in-JS codebase to a newer pattern: “In isolation or greenfield maybe it wouldn’t be a huge problem,” but in practice, it meant rewriting “whole component trees.” TheThirdRace, who had been defending the technology, answers that they had only ever evaluated it “from a greenfield project perspective,” and that it was “very enlightening to see this through the lens of a spaghetti CSS migration.”.

That is the honest version of this whole article.

Most of what we read about a fresh feature is written from the greenfield perspective. Most of what we ship is a migration.

Before you replace JavaScript with a modern CSS feature, or adopt one in an existing codebase, answer these six questions. Think of them as the conversation to have with the housemates before the newly introduced tenant gets a key. I suggest putting the answers right in the pull request description.

In a recent development, modern CSS is great and a huge improvement to styling as a whole. In particular, container queries and :has() let us express things that used to need a script, a dependency, or a hack. But a new capability does not hand us a simpler system by default. In every scenario we looked at, the new tenant did something that didn’t sit well with others, and that was because nobody introduced them to the housemates’ ways of doing things. We get a simpler system when the new rule has one clear owner, a scope we have checked, a place in the cascade we chose on purpose, and numbers showing it helped.

So, the next time a pull request deletes more than it adds, enjoy the red lines. Then ask where the complexity went, and run the six questions. If you can’t answer one of them, the migration isn’t finished yet.

  • It has been revealed that zanele Muholi, Zanele Muholi, Tembisa, Johannesburg, 2014, from Faces and Phases, ed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Content warning: this episode has some discussion of sexual and homophobic violence.

It has been revealed that zanele Muholi, Zanele Muholi, Tembisa, Johannesburg, 2014, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

Industry observers note that muholi was born in 1972 in Umlazi, Durban, South Africa and lives today in Cape Town. They are a self-described visual activist, who, since the mid-2000s, have used photography to document the lives of LGBTQ+ people, initially in South Africa, where they were born.

Zanele Muholi, Diana Cristina Nascimento Ramos, Salvador, 2025, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

They have since expanded their project around the world and work in discrete, often ongoing series that have a common aim: to respond to violence and discrimination against queer and trans communities, to reflect their defiance and resistance, and to expand their visibility in visual culture in South Africa in particular but also far beyond.

Zanele Muholi, Ashara Ekundayo, Venice, 2026, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

In a recent development, the people they depict have, since the start, been far more than sitters or subjects; they are collaborators, participants who help define the way they are represented. A crucial factor is that Muholi turns the lens onto themself. “When I position myself in my own frame,” they have said. “I do so on my own terms attempting to articulate my own way of seeing and wanting to be seen.”.

Recent findings suggest that zanele Muholi, Christine Madonsela, Daveyton, Gauteng, 2017, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

And whether it is their unflinching and tender portraits of their collaborators or their imaginative and improvised self-portraits Muholi’s photographs are always beautiful objects, with a fastidious attention to the properties and possibilities of their medium.

Sources indicate that zanele Muholi, Mantedieng ‘Mantis’ Mamabolo-Cunningham, Parktown, Johannesburg, 2018, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

They discuss the influence of their mother, who was a maker herself, and was a profound influence on one of their most notable works, Somnyama Ngonyama (2012). They reflect on the enormous impact of photographers including Rotimi Fani-Kayode, Lola Flash and Joan E. Biren, writers including Audre Lorde, and musicians including Brenda Fassie. Plus, they answer our usual questions, giving insight into their daily practices and the rhythms of their work, and reflecting on the ultimate question: what is art for?

This podcast is sponsored by Bloomberg Connects, the arts and culture platform.

Bloomberg Connects offers access to a vast range of international cultural organisations through a single click, with upcoming guides being added regularly. They includeseveral guides to institutions that have shown and collected Zanele Muholi’s work, including SFMOMA in San Francisco, Tate in the UK, the Center for Visual Arts in Denver in the US, and MEP, the Maison Européenne de la Photographie in Paris. On the guide to the MEP, you will find features on its current exhibitions. They include Penn and Fashion, exploring the photographer Irving Penn’s long association with the fashion world, in which his stripped-back style has had a lasting influence on generations of photographers. You can hear audio features on all the sections of the exhibition, from his early years at Vogue magazine in the 1940s to the photographs made when Penn was in his 90s of Karl Lagerfeld, John Galliano and Christian Lacroix. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Designing a restaurant for George Lucas might seem like an invitation to draw from the filmmaker’s extensive cinematic universe.
  • Rather than referencing the Star Wars franchise or any of Lucas’s other films, the restaurant would take its cues from something more personal: Skywalker Ranch, the filmmaker’s creative retreat in Northern California.
  • In the latest episode of Once Upon a Project, Rockwell joins host AJ Paron to discuss how that vision took shape, from the unconventional fabrication techniques behind the restaurant’s sculptural wood interior to the decisions that shaped its relationship with the surrounding museum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Designing a restaurant for George Lucas might seem like an invitation to draw from the filmmaker’s extensive cinematic universe. But when David Rockwell and his team began developing Skywalker Grill, the signature restaurant at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the conversation went in a different direction.

Rather than referencing the Star Wars franchise or any of Lucas’s other films, the restaurant would take its cues from something more personal: Skywalker Ranch, the filmmaker’s creative retreat in Northern California. Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, envisioned a space that felt warm, intimate, and welcoming, a deliberate contrast to the futuristic architecture of the museum designed by Ma Yansong of MAD Architects.

In the latest episode of Once Upon a Project, Rockwell joins host AJ Paron to discuss how that vision took shape, from the unconventional fabrication techniques behind the restaurant’s sculptural wood interior to the decisions that shaped its relationship with the surrounding museum.

“They wanted to start the conversation around warmth and the kind of warmth of Skywalker Ranch in many facets, not only material palette but also custom furniture,” Rockwell explains.

Sources indicate that that direction ultimately led to an interior defined by rich cherry wood, curved banquettes, custom furnishings, and carefully integrated lighting. One of its most striking features is a continuous wood shell that wraps from ceiling to walls, creating an almost cocoon-like environment. According to Rockwell, there isn’t a single right angle in the restaurant.

Industry observers note that achieving that effect was considerably more complicated than it appears. Each cherry wood panel was individually fabricated using a combination of traditional woodworking and technology-enabled techniques. Behind the seamless surfaces, the team also had to accommodate seismic requirements, mechanical systems, lighting, and acoustics.

Recent findings suggest that when Paron asks what proved most challenging during the project, Rockwell points to the engineering behind the wood shell. “If I had to pinpoint one element, it would be developing the system to mount and support the cherry wood panels in such an organic design,” he recalls.

The conversation also explores how the team approached the restaurant’s relationship with the surrounding museum. While the building’s sweeping forms and futuristic character could have encouraged a more theatrical interior, Rockwell and his clients were interested in something subtler.

Instead of incorporating recognizable cinematic imagery, the design borrows from filmmaking’s use of light, movement, and framing. A curved bar directs attention toward panoramic views of Los Angeles, while the lighting was carefully designed to avoid reflections in the expansive glass walls.

It has been revealed that even the furniture placement was considered from an unusually cinematic perspective: Rockwell Group created renderings from every seat in the restaurant. “We’ve never had anyone ask us to look at that from that specific point of view,” Rockwell shares.

Throughout the episode, Rockwell offers a behind-the-scenes look at his collaboration with Lucas and Hobson, who were closely involved in the design process, reviewing mockups, testing furniture, and helping shape the restaurant’s many details.

Listen to the latest episode of Once Upon a Project to hear the full conversation between host AJ Paron and David Rockwell.

This season of Once Upon a Project is presented by Crypton.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • pen.dev pairs a 60fps WebGL canvas and live shaders with browser import and two-way MCP integration for real product design.
  • Industry observers note that we've been testing pen.dev closely for quite some time, and we're ready to say it: for our daily work at Abduzeedo, it has gotten our full attention and replaced Figma in our day-to-day flow.
  • Sources indicate that the speed is truly impressive, and that speed helps you ideate more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

pen.dev pairs a 60fps WebGL canvas and live shaders with browser import and two-way MCP integration for real product design.

Industry observers note that we've been testing pen.dev closely for quite some time, and we're ready to say it: for our daily work at Abduzeedo, it has gotten our full attention and replaced Figma in our day-to-day flow. That isn't a claim we make lightly. pen.dev feels like the closest we get to designing the real product. For anyone who spends a lot of time in the browser inspector or has been coding in the past, the whole environment feels immediately familiar.

Sources indicate that the speed is truly impressive, and that speed helps you ideate more. Built on a custom WebGL renderer, the canvas stays locked at 60fps even when you throw 10,000 photos and 10GB of content at it. Panning, zooming, and nudging dense artboards feel instant, with none of the sluggishness that slows down exploration.

Sources indicate that what makes pen.dev feel like a real design tool rather than a prompt box is how much hands-on visual control you keep. You get a proper pen tool, flex layout, variables, snapping, and familiar shortcuts, alongside components with overrides and slots plus shared design systems that make it easy to manage your workflows and keep every project in sync across files. Real-time shaders, linear, radial, angular, and mesh gradients, and masking sit right inside the inspector. Having live shaders built directly into the canvas changes how quickly you can test atmosphere and depth without jumping to another app.

Sources indicate that iterating with multiple agents is where the workflow really opens up. Instead of waiting on one linear prompt thread, you can spin up parallel agents to generate side-by-side variants right on the canvas and test completely different concepts at the same time. In the Goodies view, you can see directions like Darkmatter, Brickworks, and Verdant Ark laid out next to each other as real, editable frames. Agents can also draw custom icons and illustrations directly on the same layers you edit by hand, leaving plenty of room for the happy accidents that only happen when you're moving rectangles around yourself.

Recent findings suggest that one of our favorite features is importing directly from the browser. In the age of AI, design more than ever is a two-way street. Sometimes you don't start from the design tool at all, you start from a working prototype or a live site. Being able to pull that straight into pen.dev for quick visual iterations is often way quicker and cheaper than trying to explain every tweak to an AI in words. For those of us who sometimes have a hard time translating ideas into prompts, but not into visuals, that completes the loop.

You can also pull 10 to 15 live reference sites onto the canvas in a grid, or keep your running localhost app open in a split-screen browser right beside its source design to compare spacing and typography in real time.

Where things really click for us is the two-way MCP integration. Inside the settings panel, you can wire up external MCP servers like Linear, Notion, or Mobbin so agents on the canvas pull real product specs and UI references as you design. Going the other way, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Antigravity connect to pen.dev over MCP to read your frames directly.

According to recent reports, because every project saves as an open .pen JSON file right inside your repository, coding agents build from your actual components, spacing, and variables instead of guessing from a flat screenshot. You can open the design and code side by side with the VS Code and Cursor extensions, run headless workflows through the pen.dev CLI, or use one-click export to HTML with CSS or Tailwind.

Industry observers note that design thinking stays on the canvas, and clean implementation follows right behind it. Explore the tool and try the web app at pen.dev.

Burlwood Is Making a Comeback With a Modern Twist

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few materials make a visual statement quite like burlwood.
  • In a recent development, burlwood gained popularity during the Art Deco era of the 1920s and ’30s before becoming a defining feature of furniture design in the 1970s.
  • Design Milk spoke with four designers to learn why burlwood continues to resonate and the fresh ways they’re using it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few materials make a visual statement quite like burlwood. Its swirls and naturally irregular patterns give it a depth and individuality that are difficult to replicate. That distinctive grain comes from burls, rounded growths that develop on tree trunks or branches and are often associated with injury, stress, or infection.

In a recent development, burlwood gained popularity during the Art Deco era of the 1920s and ’30s before becoming a defining feature of furniture design in the 1970s. Today, it’s experiencing another moment. Yet its current appeal is less about recreating the past and more about rethinking how the material fits modern spaces.

Design Milk spoke with four designers to learn why burlwood continues to resonate and the fresh ways they’re using it.

Bookmatched burlwood creates a striking symmetrical pattern across this three-drawer chest, set against a sculptural curved wood bed frame. Photography by Emily Hart.

Recent findings suggest that “Burlwood does what a great print does,” says Tiffany Brooks, principal designer of Tiffany Brooks Interiors. “It gives your eye somewhere to go. Up close, you see all these little swirls and knots, and from across the room, it reads as one rich surface. Even two pieces made from the same wood can have completely different personalities.”.

Abbe Fenimore, owner of Studio Ten 25, shares that appreciation for burlwood’s organic qualities, seeing the material as a way to introduce visual interest without relying on patterned textiles.

The tightly patterned grain of this burlwood chest extends across its drawer fronts, while colorful glass candlesticks and art books add color to the display. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Industry observers note that for Eddie Maestri, founder, principal, and creative director of Maestri Studio, burlwood’s appeal lies in its departure from the predictable. “To me, the imperfections are the beauty,” he claims. “Every piece of burl is different, and you can’t fake it.”.

The designers we spoke to see burlwood as having staying power, particularly as homeowners move toward spaces that feel more personal and collected.

It has been revealed that “The material is timeless,” Brooks notes. “What changes is how we use it. Right now, I think people are a little tired of rooms that look like they all came from the same inspiration board. Burl brings some individuality back.”.

It has been revealed that A honey-toned burlwood table features a richly figured top and tapered legs, standing out against the darker wood cabinetry behind it. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Industry observers note that fenimore sees a similar appeal in burlwood’s ability to bridge different eras and styles. Its balance of modern and vintage sensibilities, she explains, can give even a brand-upcoming piece the character of something collected over time.

Maestri points to its long history, from French cabinetmakers to the Art Deco era and the 1970s, as evidence of its enduring draw. “It keeps coming back because people want warmth and things made by hand,” he states, noting that burlwood can bring a sense of soul to interiors that otherwise feel overly polished.

Walnut, maple, and mappa burl each bring a different quality to a piece, with variations in color, grain, and visual weight influencing how designers use them.

Brooks reaches for walnut burl when she wants to introduce depth and create a moodier atmosphere, while maple burl offers similar movement in a lighter, softer palette. For a bolder grain pattern, she favors mappa burl.

A burlwood nightstand introduces warmth and a touch of traditional detail to this otherwise contemporary bedroom, adding a rich wood accent against the sculptural charcoal headboard and modern lines. Photography by Nick Sargent.

Sources indicate that maestri, meanwhile, has a clear go-to: mappa burl, also known as poplar burl. “It’s my favorite because it’s lighter and more golden than walnut, so you get all that movement without the room feeling heavy,” he claims.

Sources indicate that while Mimi Meacham, founder and principal designer of Marian Louise Designs, gravitates toward rich walnut burl and lighter mappa burl, the individual piece matters more to her than the wood species. “The color, scale of the figuring, and finish all affect how it will feel in a room,” she says. “I want the grain and the shape of the furniture to complement each other.”.

Recent findings suggest that A close-up reveals the distinctive natural markings of a burlwood table, with brass-and-acrylic drawer pulls adding a mix of warm and modern finishes. Photography by Emily Hart.

Recent findings suggest that because burlwood already has so much movement, surrounding colors and finishes can either complement its natural pattern or create an intriguing contrast. Brooks likes combining burl with warm brass, matte paint, and textiles such as nubby linen and velvet. “I’d put a honey-toned burl next to a deep aubergine or an inky blue in a heartbeat,” she states. Fenimore also likes pairing burl with color and pattern, especially soft blues, olive greens, warm neutrals, and even unexpected pops of pink or red.

A burlwood tray with a gold-toned rim highlights the wood’s warm coloring and varied markings, with stacked books providing a colorful backdrop. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Sources indicate that meacham gravitates toward warm wood tones paired with blues and greens, from soft periwinkle to deep green, along with antique brass, linen, velvet, and plaster. She also considers the finish of the burl itself when choosing surrounding materials. A glossy burlwood surface, for example, can be balanced by a matte wall or softly textured fabric.

For a warmer, earthier direction, Maestri recommends tobacco, ochre, olive, and soft plaster white, complemented by brass, stone, linen, and mohair. He also prefers finishes with a subtle luster to emphasize the grain’s richness. Fenimore likes the contrast burlwood creates with lacquered surfaces, brass, upholstery, and contemporary furniture silhouettes.

A curved burlwood console showcases the wood’s richly varied grain across its drawer fronts and rounded frame, with pale green stools and white fringe adding a touch of color and texture. Photography by Emily Hart.

Industry observers note that burlwood is finding its way into a wider range of applications throughout the home. Brooks likes seeing it incorporated into architectural details, such as the back of a kitchen island or as an inset on a painted door. “A little restraint makes the detail feel more special,” she states. For larger pieces, she points to Worlds Away for its clean-lined interpretations of burlwood, as well as Ambella Home, Chairish, and 1stDibs for finding distinctive designs.

Maestri also appreciates seeing burl used beyond traditional furniture, including on lamp bases, picture frames, and cabinet doors. At home, he has a burlwood bar cabinet from Soho Home, and he’s drawn to the brand’s Wallace collection, which uses mappa burl in sculptural, curved forms.

A burlwood coffee table showcases the wood’s warm tones and naturally irregular markings, while art books and a decorative bowl give the tabletop a relaxed, collected feel. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Contemporary furniture designs also explore the interplay between burlwood, contrasting materials, and simpler silhouettes. Jonathan Adler’s Bond collection, for example, combines burl with acrylic on a dresser and metal on a dining table. Meacham points to Made Goods’ Bradley mirror, which lets the mappa burl frame take center stage. Fenimore recommends looking at brands like Modway and TOV Furniture, particularly for smaller items such as chairs, ottomans, and drink tables with burl accents.

The rich, swirling grain of the half-moon burlwood console complements the delicate branches and floral motifs in the botanical artwork above. Photography by Emily Hart.

For anyone hesitant to introduce such a distinctive material, the designers recommend beginning with one piece, such as a side table, mirror, or tray. Brooks suggests starting with something that serves an existing need, even if it’s as small as a drink table next to a chair. Maestri puts it simply: “Pick one piece and let it be the star. Keep what’s around it simpler so the grain can stand out.”.

In a recent development, fenimore encourages mixing burlwood with other wood tones rather than trying to match everything. She also sees the material as a way to ground a room that already has plenty of color and pattern. Meacham recommends giving the grain some breathing room through intentional styling and a variety of finishes. “That doesn’t mean everything else needs to be neutral—I love burl with color—but you want your eye to have somewhere to rest.”.

Burlwood’s latest resurgence doesn’t require a revival of any particular decorating style. The same material that characterized Art Deco cabinetry and 1970s furniture feels equally at home alongside contemporary silhouettes, unexpected colors, and contrasting finishes. Its history is part of its appeal, but it needn’t dictate how we use it.

Industry observers note that colleen Sullivan is a lifestyle writer and editor who specializes in home, travel, beauty, fashion, food, weddings, and wellness. She’s a contributor at multiple digital publications, and served as a print editor at Vogue, Working Woman, Health, and HGTV. When Colleen isn’t working, she loves to restore old beach houses at the Jersey Shore. Sullivan also serves as an adjunct professor at the Newhouse School at Syracuse University.

Tech Report: Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible

  • In a recent development, I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that eric is a Boston-based designer who helps create straightforward solutions that address a person’s practical, physical, cognitive, and emotional needs. More about Eric ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career. Now I want to share this knowledge with you.

Accessibility is a core part of a functional digital experience. As the LLM chat pattern continues to spread like wildfire across the web, we risk excluding people if these experiences are not built with accessibility as a core consideration.

It is also worth re-mentioning what “exclusion” means here: It’s the loss of knowledge, the loss of opportunity, the loss of utility, the loss of employability, the loss of entertainment, and more.

“Immersive LLM chat experience” is a catch-all term for full-screen experiences like Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, America.gov, Glean, and other similar websites and web apps:.

The majority of what this post covers applies to both web apps and native apps. This is because these experiences are typically built using web technologies, then placed in a native wrapper via frameworks such as Electron or Tauri.

Sources indicate that immersive LLM chat experiences are not patterns such as a pop-up chat, inline text generation utilities, or summarization tools. These simpler applications of LLM technology will have different considerations and expectations. Instead, this is a starting point for making those other experiences accessible.

In a recent development, there is nothing special about chat-based UIs when viewed via the lens of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. They are interactive experiences, built using web technologies. The losses I’ve described — and the legal liability associated with them — are access barriers in the same way any other web content can be an access barrier.

I would also like to mention the social model of disability here: the idea that exclusion can be created by the built environment. For example, consider an elevated entryway that uses a gently sloping ramp in place of stairs.

It has been revealed that built environments also extend to digital experiences, and the social model also applies here. The main activities undertaken to operate an LLM chat are already well-established:.

It is how we facilitate — or fail to facilitate — those interactions that’s the salient bit.

Before we get into the technical aspects, we must consider the overwhelming visual bias that permeates software creation.

In a recent development, we live in a highly visual culture, so our outputs unconsciously reflect and reinforce that. What we need to do here is be aware of and think through the non-visual considerations.

While not all disabilities are blindness or low vision conditions, a lot of the core interactions of an LLM chat do need specific accommodations for these two types of disability.

In a recent development, recall the social model of disability here, and how it applies to the main flow of using an LLM-based chat. You:.

Let’s demonstrate at a high level what someone who can fully see the screen experiences compared to someone who uses a screen reader and cannot see the entire screen, or large portions of it:.

Visually, we can see the LLM reply appear. Someone who uses a screen reader does not know newly introduced content has appeared because:.

Sources indicate that so, how do we create an experience for someone who uses a screen reader that is equivalent to the experience of someone who can fully see the screen? To start, we use live regions.

Live region announcements will enable someone to know what the LLM has responded with without having to move focus from the input used for prompting. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, glancing upwards to read the LLM response when it appears.

It has been revealed that first, read this excellent article by TetraLogical if this is your first attempt at getting live region announcements working. They’re tricky to get right, and this article sets the record straight.

In a recent development, one common pitfall I want to call specific attention to is applying aria-live on each LLM response message. Don’t do this. Instead, use a dedicated live region area to announce each message’s content.

According to recent reports, the live region area should be placed at the end of the DOM and used for all live region messaging. This method is far more stable and reliable, which is key for ensuring everyone understands what the experience is communicating.

With that established: What we want to do is trigger a live region announcement when the LLM’s chat reply highlights up in full on the screen.

This creates an outcome where you can read the message if you can see the screen, and hear or feel the message if you cannot.

There are a few things to do when creating a good user experience for the people who rely on these live region announcements. These considerations mean the difference between a compliant-yet-unusable outcome and something that genuinely works for the person using it.

Attempting to announce the message as it streams in may create a juddering and confusing experience that’s difficult for someone to parse.

It is better to wait until the message has completed streaming, and then announce the message’s content in full.

Recent findings suggest that responses from an LLM often take time to complete. Generally speaking, there are three ways to show a response is still processing:.

These experiences are typically only shown visually. If you cannot see the screen, it may lead to it feeling like the experience has stalled or crashed — especially if the response is for a large or complicated request that takes a while to work through.

To address this, we’ll want to use live region announcements:.

If text is visually shown on the screen: Ensure a companion live region announcement is also triggered at the same time the loading message text is displayed. The text string for the live region announcement should be the same as what is shown visually, to be sure to ensure parity of experience:.

If a text-less loading animation is shown on the screen: Ensure the loading state is also communicated to assistive technology.

A live region announcement that mentions the reply is loading after a set amount of time will facilitate an equivalent experience for this interaction. It doesn’t have to be too verbose; the word “Loading” can suffice:.

Industry observers note that triggering the loading message five seconds after prompt submission seems to be the sweet spot, according to the inclusive user research I evaluated. You can then have your logic repeat the loading message every five seconds until the LLM completes its actual reply.

Be sure to also announce the reply immediately as it finishes streaming. You don’t need to wait until the next five-second loading message cycle is complete.

Also consider randomly selecting from a set of different phrases that communicate that a response is being formulated after the initial “Loading” message is dispatched. This helps in scenarios where someone may think the loading experience itself has crashed or stalled.

We’ll eventually be able to replace the technique TetraLogical outlined with ariaNotify(). It is a much-needed and welcome addition to the platform, and will drastically lower the hacks and headaches many developers encounter when creating and managing live region announcements.

In a recent development, baseline lists the ariaNotify() method as having cross-browser availability at the time of this article’s publication. However, there are two factors to consider here:.

Also consider that while a polyfill for ariaNotify() is available, you need to factor in whether it has both:.

What this realistically means is holding off for a while on ariaNotify() in favor of the tried and true TetraLogical live region technique.

Industry observers note that headings are the most popular way people who use screen readers navigate around an experience. Because of this, I advocate for inserting visually-hidden headings before each chat message.

Here’s a simplified version of that in code:.

And here’s what the code might look like using the actual content from a human question and an LLM response:.

In a recent development, so, why the “You said:”/”Cody said:” prefix? Remember the visual bias. Visually, we can see the left- or right-hand alignment of messages, used to indicate who is saying what.

Industry observers note that the prefix serves the same purpose: identifying the message’s owner. This allows people to promptly move through a conversation the same way someone might quickly scroll upwards to re-establish context, checking who said what and when.

Using landmark regions to wrap the larger overall areas of your LLM chat experience helps people understand its overall layout. It can also enable quick screen reader navigation to each area:.

Industry observers note that landmarks allow someone who cannot see the screen to learn about its overall makeup. This is the equivalent of how we quickly move our eyes and tilt our heads to different overall areas when scanning the screen to initially learn the overall layout of an experience.

Industry observers note that I am hesitant to wrap chat messages in section or other landmark elements. The reason for this is that they “pollute” the list of landmarks a screen reader can generate, making navigation more laborious. This is especially relevant for long-running sessions where many messages are present.

Compare the following and ask yourself which one would be easier to move through with your keyboard if trying to jump from the prompt content area back to the sessions area:.

Here, our visually hidden heading elements serve as a dedicated navigation mechanism for moving through the LLM conversation.

In addition to headings and landmarks, there are two other ways to let people get around promptly:.

Skip links — sometimes referred to as skip navigation — allow you to quickly jump to another area on the same page or view.

Skip to main content links are commonplace on many mature websites and web apps. Immersive LLM chat experiences should be no different.

Place a skip link in the DOM that allows someone to jump to the main conversation area before any other DOM content that is shown visually on the screen.

Also consider using additional skip links that enable:.

Recent findings suggest that composite widgets are used when a discrete section of content contains multiple interactive elements. Focus is then managed within this section by the developer, so that:.

Industry observers note that for the purposes of an immersive LLM chat experience, we want to make conversation lists composite widgets. This enables someone to swiftly navigate both within and past the entire list.

According to recent reports, here, consider the use case of someone who exclusively relies on a keyboard to navigate. Compare pressing Tab 50 times to get through each of the 50 conversation sessions you’ve created versus pressing Tab once. Now consider motor control conditions where those keypresses can be fatiguing, or even painful to perform.

Once someone places focus on a conversation list composite widget, they can use the Up and Down arrow keys to navigate through each conversation session list item.

As a quality-of-life improvement, I also like to support the following keyboard interactions:.

To save you a lot of headaches and prototyping: Corner cases around focus management and usability expectations for people who rely exclusively on keyboards work against you if you try to go with a feed pattern approach.

There’s no need to unnecessarily overcomplicate things. The article elements’ wrapping messages with visually-hidden headings approach that I’ve described earlier is both simple and effective.

People who use assistive technology understand the simpler approach, and it involves far less effort to maintain. It’s a win-win!

Industry observers note that pressing F6/Shift+F6 to hop around different areas of the app is an older navigation technique some people who use Windows screen readers employ when navigating through installable desktop apps. Think of it a lot like navigating by landmark.

Recent findings suggest that LLM chat experiences are effectively apps in their own right. Because of this, we can recreate the F6 navigation experience and accommodate those who might attempt it. That means:.

It has been revealed that there’s no secret sauce here. For starters, place an id on each landmark, as well as tabindex="-1". Also ensure each landmark other than main has an accessible name, granted via either aria-label or aria-labelledby.

In a recent development, after that, have an event listener set up to recognize Control+F6 and Control+Shift+F6 key presses. Set focus to:.

Recent findings suggest that and voilà! We now have web-based F6 navigation.

As it is an older technique, people who are younger or less experienced with screen readers may not know F6 navigation exists.

According to recent reports, consider socializing the capability in the accessibility portion of your application’s settings menu to address this lack of awareness. Also consider exposing and making F6 navigation re-bindable as another discovery technique, provided your application supports keyboard shortcut rebinding.

Industry observers note that again, this advice only applies to an immersive LLM chat experience. Help agent popups and other less-sophisticated experiences have different expectations.

There are two areas that deserve more finesse when considering where to set focus when F6 navigation is used: the prompting input and the conversation.

Setting focus directly on the input used to type prompts — and not its parent form landmark element — allows someone to quickly get into the action.

Similarly, setting focus on the visually hidden heading of the last message displayed allows them to swiftly jump to the content the LLM generated — a data attribute such as data-last-message can be really helpful for managing this.

Using F6 and Shift+F6 keypresses allows someone to hop from the chat input to what the LLM outputs, then back again. This enables rapid keyboard-based review and iteration on an LLM’s output.

Adjust the text size of your experience and double-check that content is not clipped, or that there’s horizontal overflow.

According to recent reports, people increase the text size of the experiences they use, and more than you’d probably guess. They also resize application windows. Also consider that most LLM-based chat designs tend to use a smaller text size to allow for more information shown on screen.

Because of these two factors, it makes sense to evaluate how your experience holds up when the browser font size is increased.

In a recent development, customization lives at the heart of accessibility. It’s only natural that LLM-based chat experiences have preferences to better accommodate all the different ways people use them.

In that vein, thoughtful preference offerings can go a long way to helping out people with access needs. Here are some that I’ve found to be particularly useful.

Industry observers note that some LLMs perform interim actions that are circumstantially less important than the messages they ultimately generate. Here, consider programming-oriented LLMs. They can perform actions like researching and reasoning, code search, and tool calls.

Sources indicate that these secondary actions typically have a smaller, less visually key treatment compared to the messages that contain the main LLM response content. This is because the results are more important than the methodology when using this type of interaction.

Announcing each of these secondary actions could lead to a confusing or overwhelming experience, especially if multiple actions are clustered and fire off live messages in rapid succession.

To address this, you can allow people to circumstantially switch off the announcements for this type of ancillary information. The content in the conversation is still present; it just isn’t unveiled via a live region. This is equivalent to how someone who can see the screen can skim over them.

Letting someone re-enable these types of announcements also grants parity in experience, in that it allows them to know the actions are happening if they want a more information-intensive experience. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, intentionally paying close attention to the LLM’s actions.

Sources indicate that it might also be worth investigating letting people toggle visually hiding and showing these less vital announcements, as well. This can help people with attention or cognitive considerations, who may be less familiar with technical jargon.

Loading animations and large animated effects, like streaming conversations and side panels expanding and collapsing, can be distracting for some people with attention and cognitive considerations. That can go a long way toward breaking someone’s flow.

To address this, you can provide a toggle to turn off animations, reducing their transition time to zero.

You should also strive to be a respectful and courteous steward of the experience. Default your animation toggle to an off state if a request for a reduced motion experience has been in the device operating system. You can use the prefers-reduced-motion media feature to achieve this. Also consider a setting that can re-enable animation, even if a reduced motion request is present.

Sources indicate that some people can get distracted by, or have their focus disrupted by, sound effects. This is similar to animation considerations.

According to recent reports, letting people turn off app-specific sound effects means they don’t have to mute their entire device. Here, consider things like other apps playing flow state-inducing music or white noise that they might be using to help them focus.

Alternatives for sound-based notifications include, but are not limited to:.

I am of the school of thought that any experience that uses keyboard shortcuts also needs to allow both editing and being switched off, both in bulk and on a shortcut-by-shortcut basis.

You may be quick to think of conflicts with assistive technology, but I’d also like to take this space to remind you of different language keyboard layouts.

According to recent reports, live region messages are plain text strings. These strings are announced by screen readers in full in one go from start to end.

Sources indicate that semantic information that comes for free by using the appropriate HTML element isn’t present in live region announcements—it’s stripped out. Because of that, we need to think about how we could make our live region content both clear and useful.

Each type of special content has its own considerations. For my work, I created special cases for tables and blocks of code:.

A table’s cell content will sound odd when revealed without the companion semantic structure conferred by elements such as table, th, tr, and td. Relationships between columns and rows aren’t present in a live region announcement, either.

Because of this, we can convert the live region announcement of tables to use a concise description of the number of rows and columns, plus a general description and overall trends it might highlight.

A block of code sounds like gibberish when the line breaks are stripped away, and the content is flattened into a single string.

And if it’s a large block of code, it can be a tedious amount of gibberish to parse — nobody wants to sit through an announcement of 2,376 lines of code, painstakingly announced character-by-character.

To accommodate this, we can convert the live region announcement of code blocks to use the filename or file type, plus how many lines of code the block contains.

Also note here that people can revisit the actual message content itself. The actual message content will ideally have the appropriate semantics applied to it. This means things like tables being announced as, and navigated through as, table content.

In this way, the live region message is a context-setting preview of what to expect. This is the equivalent of quickly visually skimming a message as it is streaming in, then scrolling back to review its content with more attention afterward.

Recent findings suggest that all of the previous is built atop feedback from testing different approaches and noting what works, and what could be improved. You want to facilitate disabled people being the experts in their own lived experience, and not treat others’ advice as the more credible source.

Inclusive user research is a vital way of determining if an experience is actually usable. Centering disabled people’s observations and perspectives is a way to take an experience beyond baseline compliance and create something usable and equitable.

It is vital to ensure that everyone can use chat-based LLM interactions as the pattern continues to proliferate. Although this is not an exhaustive list of everything you’ll need to do, the content above covers a wide swath of the main places accessibility barriers and friction may show up.

It is my sincerest hope that the improvements I’ve learned about and implemented can help you with your efforts to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who use assistive technology to get what they want or need online.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emiglia brand identity by Another Collective: a hand-cut red wordmark, script lettering and windowed packs for a Porto pasta maker and bar.

The rebrand unifies two sides of one business, the Pasta Fresca factory and the Pasta Bar, under a single voice. The studio kept the illustrations that were already part of the brand and built a stronger typographic layer around them, so tradition reads as confidence rather than nostalgia. Red does most of the work, a warm tomato red against cream, with deep burgundy as the second voice. The pasta itself reveals up everywhere, nests on steel trays, boxes with windows, trays stacked in the fridge, and the identity treats that craft as the subject, not the backdrop.

The wordmark is the whole idea in one gesture. Chunky, rounded letters with soft terminals and slightly uneven edges, the kind of letterforms that look cut by hand rather than drawn on screen. It sits huge and flat, filling the width of posters and packs, with the round counter of the A and the arched legs of the M giving it a warmth no geometric sans could carry.

In a recent development, under it, a loose handwritten script spells out Pasta Fresca or Pasta Bar, and a small typewriter-style caps line carries the facts: massas, molhos, refeiÃ§Ãµes prontas, kits. The order never changes. Wordmark first, script second, small caps last, and the same order repeats on boxes, menus, bags and tees.

In a recent development, the packaging puts the pasta on display. Red boxes carry a clear window so the shapes inside do the talking, with a small illustrated label on each box. Foil trays stack in the fridge under bold red labels, and the same red runs across paper bags, sauce jars and the weekly menu posters.

In the bar, the system turns physical. Menus in red and burgundy sit on steel counters, plates carry a thin red rim with the name set small, and the staff tees carry the house line, Thereâs No Cream In Carbonara, flanked by two small Emiglia badges. From packaging to signage to menus, every piece pulls in the same direction.

Rabbithole revamps London Film Schoolâs branding with Kimeraâs Waldenburg type, a brighter red, and stark framing bars across print and web.

It has been revealed that one solid black bar sits directly above three tightly stacked lines of condensed type, pressed glossy into textured red paper. Itâs a blunt opening move. According to Visuelle, studio Rabbithole built this branding and an in-house website to reconnect London Film School with the independent, anti-establishment spirit it established in 1956. Thereâs no decorative crest or nostalgic film-reel icon softening the cover. Rabbithole anchors the mark in Kimeraâs Waldenburg, using the narrow, heavy Waldenburg Schwer Schmal cut shown on the print proof sheet â packing dense weight into a tight vertical rectangle. That rectangular bar works like a cropped frame edge, signaling a filmmakerâs viewfinder before a single sentence gets read.

That bar doesnât stay horizontal for long. On the animated black poster grid, white bars snap to the vertical edges beside left- and right-aligned LONDON FILM SCHOOL stacks while a central stroke tilts across faint gridlines and swaps the name for LFS.ORG.UK. The modular layout takes every shift cleanly. On the scan print test sheet, Rabbithole places the brighter, digital-ready red straight across four contrasting film stills: a sunlit beach, soldiers walking down a dusk road, a winter lake, and a figure lying on dark forest leaves. Even over a rotated black-and-white archival street photo labeled Colour marque on image [F], the saturated red block cuts through busy photographic grain. Five stepped coral-to-red tint swatches and heavy double chevrons keep the print specs strictly utilitarian.

It has been revealed that physical campus items strip the branding down to heavy fabric and stark contrast. On the matte black canvas tote, the bar stretches wide along the bottom seam right above a single red line of type, leaving the upper bag open. The stacked rectangular patches go tighter still. Dense black satin-stitch embroidery packs just LFS into woven red frames edged in matching red thread, letting the condensed characters hold clean counters over coarse fabric grain. As Visuelle notes, Rabbithole also designed and built the fresh website in-house to give prospective international students a clearer platform. Whether stitched onto a jacket patch or stretched across the base of a canvas tote, that lone bar and condensed cut tie the branding back to the 1956 school.

You might have already read my name every now and then here at Smashing Magazine. I’m Paul Boag. I’ve written three books with Smashing and 77 articles (yes, I counted), and I sit on Smashing’s advisory board.

In a recent development, so when Vitaly and the Smashing team offered me this slot in your inbox, I didn’t take it lightly. I want to tell you about something I’m launching in January with Smashing as my partner, and why I think it matters right now.

Every year I talk to hundreds of people working in digital. Some work in-house, some run agencies, and some freelance. And the same thing comes up again and again. The hardest part of the job usually isn’t the design work. It’s everything around it.

The stakeholder who redesigns things in the review meeting. The business case sitting in someone’s inbox. The project that has been “about to start” since last spring. And now, the senior manager who has read that AI can do user research in an afternoon.

What makes it harder is that a lot of us deal with all this on our own. Many are a team of one, or a team of a few.

Their colleagues are great, but they work in the same organization with the same blind spots. Nobody down the corridor has dealt with this before.

It has been revealed that what’s missing is an outside view. Someone who has dealt with the same awful stakeholder and can tell you how they handled it.

Sources indicate that most of us rarely get that conversation, and the job is changing faster than ever. There’s very little established best practice for working with AI yet. Everyone is figuring it out at once, mostly alone.

UX Insiders is a small, paid community for people doing UX inside organizations. Designers, researchers, UX leads, and anyone championing UX where they work, whatever their job title.

Christie's declared today it has acquired the British auction house Dreweatts, a move that confirms the enduring appeal of antiques and older collectibles, particularly as profits in other parts of the auction sector remain squeezed.

Both businesses will run as before, Christie’s confirms, with no staffing changes expected as a result of the deal. Dreweatts will retain its name and continue to be run “independently” by its chief executive, Henry House, and chairman Will Richards, according to a Christie's statement. Dreweatts will continue to operate from its salesroom at Donnington Priory in Newbury, Berkshire, with no sales expected to move to London.

Dreweatts, founded in 1759, is best known for country house and estate sales, and its specialist departments covering furniture, Old Masters, ceramics, jewellery, silver, clocks and wine. It holds around 70 sales a year. In 2025, it posted a record total auction turnover of £37.56m (£47.3m with fees)—a 26% increase from its 2024 results. Both Christie’s and Dreweatts are privately owned and do not disclose their profits.

A display ahead of the sale of Patrick and Amabel Lindsay’s collection at Dreweatts.

The acquisition in some ways sees Christie’s backtrack its 2017 decision to close its South Kensington venue, known as Christie's South Kensington or CSK, which specialised in antiques and other traditional collecting categories. This decision was taken as the market for postwar and contemporary art was at its peak, and as the trade chased global expansion and billionaire tastes at the expense of localism and connoisseurship.

According to recent reports, today, auctions of Modern and postwar trophy lots might generate more glamour and headlines than high-volume and lower-value antiques sales, but the overheads for winning these prize consignments devours profit margins. Indeed, many leading industry figures criticised Christie’s decision to close CSK as a shortsighted one that haemorrhaged valuable strongholds of specialist knowledge and alienated potential upcoming buyers.

Christie's president Bonnie Brennan claims in a statement that Dreweatts possesses “particular strength in a part of the market that is highly complementary to our own. Most importantly, our clients collect across categories and at every price point, and together we have the opportunity to provide them with an even broader and more complete level of service.”.

This marks the second major acquisition of a smaller auction house by Christie’s in recent years, following the 2024 buyout of the classic car vendors Gooding & Tech giant.

According to recent reports, christie’s acquires Dreweatts from the advisory firm Gurr Johns, which bought the regional auction house in 2017 for £1.25m, as The Art Newspaper reported at the time. “I believe that Christie’s is the only business with the capacity, experience and shared culture to fulfil the further potential of Dreweatts,”, Gurr Johns chief told the Financial Times.

#206280. Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams
